events.title: Cramer says 'frozen' conditions are holding many stocks back. Here's what could change that
events.summary: CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that investors need to stay in the market despite "frozen" conditions in key industries. He pointed to housing, capital markets, and the data center boom as examples. CNBC's Jim Cramer said Wednesday that investors shouldn't jump ship despite signs of slowing activity across key parts of the economy. Cramer's comments come as high interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty and political opposition weigh on stocks across industries. The U.S. housing market remains mired in a multiyear period of sluggishness, IPO and M&A activity has slowed , and even the booming data-center buildout is facing new obstacles — leaving fewer catalysts to drive crucial parts of the market higher. "Market after market is getting frozen right now and that's killing stocks," the " Mad Money " host said. Housing is perhaps the clearest example. The 30-year mortgage rate has climbed to roughly 7.5%, from about 3% five years ago, leaving many homeowners locked into cheaper mortgages reluctant or unable to move. "The nearly 7.5% mortgage has made housing the least affordable it's been in 40 years," Cramer said. The slowdown has rippled across housing-related stocks, including homebuilders Lennar and KB Home and retailers Home Depot and Lowe's , both of which hit fresh 52-week lows on Wednesday. Fewer home sales also mean less spending on appliances, furniture and renovations, pressuring stocks like Whirlpool , which also hit a 52-week low Wednesday. Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by the CNBC Investing Club, owns shares of Home Depot. Once-booming capital markets are also showing signs of slowing. Cramer pointed to smart ring maker Oura's decision to postpone its planned $2.2 billion IPO , as well as Dunkin Donuts and Buffalo Wild Wings' parent Inspire Brands shelving its own offering . "Without IPOs or M&A, the huge banking cohort is frozen except for fees," Cramer said. "That's just not good enough." Even the booming data-center industry faces new obstacles as political concerns around electricity costs and other impacts threaten to slow development. The stakes are raised by this being a midterm election year, with Democrats and Republicans vying for control of Congress. But Cramer cautioned investors against abandoning the market because headwinds can quickly turn into tailwinds. Most notably, an end to the war could push oil and inflation lower, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to take another interest rate hike off the table and unleashing a powerful stock rally. "It could happen in three quick days, perhaps the three most important days of 2026," Cramer said. "That's why I hesitate to leave the market at this moment." If the economy starts to thaw, Cramer concluded, "then you get a virtual running of the bulls." events.title: Nation's love affair with coffee on shaky ground as cost of living bites
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Price hikes force more Australians to make coffee at home to save money Glenn Jones is a chief coffee taster at a Queensland coffee processing plant. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) October 1 is International Coffee Day, which celebrates the global significance of the popular beverage. Nestlé Australia, which produces instant coffee, says there has been a surge in sales. Cost-of-living pressures are forcing more coffee lovers to change their spending habits amid rising cafe prices. At a Queensland coffee-processing factory, 10 people are employed to ensure every batch tastes exactly as it should. Each day they gather in groups of three or four around a rotating table that has a few sinks on the side so they can spit out the samples as they go. "We do sample up to 100 cups per day, so you don't want to be drinking that much coffee on a standard day," quality assurance manager or "chief taste-tester" for Nestlé, Glenn Jones, said. Nestlé Australia's Gympie factory employs 10 tasters who sample the coffee every day. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) The factory in Gympie, about two hours' drive north of Brisbane, has been producing instant coffee since 1997. Mr Jones said even though drinking the beverage was part of his job description, he also enjoyed it when he was off-duty. "I need coffee before I come to work in the morning, then I taste it all day, and I'll have coffee on the weekends — I love coffee," he said. Glenn Jones still drinks coffee outside of work hours. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) Mr Jones is not alone in his obsession, with an estimated three-quarters of Australians consuming coffee regularly. Data shows more than 5 million Australians visit a cafe daily for their caffeine hit. Martin Brown says cappuccino sachets have been the "fastest-growing part of the market" in the past five years. ( Supplied. ) But Martin Brown, general manager of Nestlé's coffee and dairy business, said the company's sales figures showed a shift back to home consumption. "[Australia has] one of the most sophisticated coffee cultures in the world, but we also have a cost-of-living challenge at the moment," Mr Brown said. "A lot of households are having to make choices and find smarter ways to buy things." He said cappuccino sachets had been the "fastest-growing part of the market" in the past five years, but there was also a shift back to more "traditional" soluble instant coffee. "A cup of Blend 43 will cost you 12 to 15 cents a cup … it's super convenient and it's value for money and none of that goes out of fashion," he said. Nestlé Australia's Gympie processing plant produces about 20 million cups of coffee each day. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 3 per cent in the 12 months leading up to August this year, with meals out and takeaway prices up 4.5 per cent. The average price of a cafe-bought flat white in Australia is now about $6 a cup, despite warnings it could soar to double digits this year. University students (from left) Elora Hemmer, Charlotte Cairns and Holly Durbidge have cut back on buying coffee out. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) On Queensland's Sunshine Coast, university student Charlotte Cairns said it was even more expensive to buy a cold coffee. "I feel like when a coffee is $5 it's like, 'Oh, that's alright'," Ms Cairns said. Deann Mayfield said she and her partner had started to limit the amount of coffee they bought out. "It's very expensive. We have one special coffee a day, so we try not to double up," Ms Mayfield said. Deann Mayfield says she feels for cafe owners, who were also dealing with rising costs. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) Coffee bean prices reached record highs last year , forcing importers and roasters to raise their prices, which was ultimately passed on to customers. While green bean prices have dropped in 2026, they remain three times higher than in 2021. More than five million Australians visit a cafe or coffee shop every day. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) Australian Specialty Coffee Association president Bruno Maiolo said the drop had not offset the increase in "all of the other costs", including rent, electricity, milk and wages. "We have a one-in-two failure rate [for coffee businesses]," Mr Maiolo said. "People are going broke, not because they're necessarily bad operators; it's because they cannot keep the margins that are required to stay in business. Bruno Maiolo says it is a challenging time to be in the cafe business.

events.title: Inside Zuckerberg, Huang's push for White House AI pact
events.summary: Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg looks at President Donald Trump as he holds a press briefing with tech executives following a meeting on AI. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Mark Zuckerberg was the chief architect of the AI accords that emerged from Trump's lunch with tech leaders, POLITICO reports. Zuckerberg, with the help of Jensen Huang, pitched the AI accords to senior White House officials at the lunch. Huang and some Trump administration officials helped shape the pact ahead of the meeting. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg was the chief architect of the "morally binding" AI accords that emerged from Tuesday's White House lunch with President Donald Trump, Speaker Mike Johnson, and more than a dozen tech executives, according to five people familiar with the private meeting. Zuckerberg, with the help of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, pitched the so-called AI accords to senior White House officials and some of the biggest names in tech during the luncheon, three of the people said. Both Huang as well as Trump administration officials helped shape the pact ahead of the meeting, according to two of the people. All five people were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to share details of the discussions. As part of the  voluntary agreement , signatories would commit to the importance of enacting safeguards to mitigate potential risks from advanced AI models, but without a clear enforcement mechanism, it is unclear what, if any, consequences they may face for failing to do so. The episode indicates Zuckerberg and Huang's growing influence shaping White House AI policy, and comes as the administration continues to pursue a light-touch approach to regulating the technology. Congress has yet to pass federal legislation reining in AI. Meta declined to comment. Nvidia and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The idea originated at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping, during which Zuckerberg pitched the idea to Johnson, one of the people said. Shortly thereafter, Zuckerberg spoke with Huang who subsequently helped to garner support for it among leadership at the major AI labs, according to two of the people. Since the state dinner until Tuesday's luncheon, executives have been in consistent communication to finalize the document. Semafor previously reported some of the details of the document's creation. The accords compel companies to "implement robust internal controls" to monitor AI models' capabilities, partner with external auditors, and create independent committees to review the auditors' reports. It has been criticized by some Democrats and safety advocates who say it is unenforceable and relies primarily on mutual agreement. "The idea isn't that this is the only thing that we will ever do," Zuckerberg told reporters outside the White House Tuesday. "It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to." Trump has been reluctant to impose additional guardrails on the technology, saying that existing laws will be enough to mitigate the risks the technology may pose. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," Trump said in a post on Truth Social earlier this month. As the White House has weighed how best to regulate AI, Zuckerberg has favored a lighter-touch approach. In an August phone call with Trump, Zuckerberg opposed a proposal that would create an independent regulatory body modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. Huang has positioned himself as a coalition builder within the industry. On Monday, Nvidia released a new AI security system the company said would help prevent recent autonomous hacks conducted by rogue AI agents that have made headlines. Other top tech executives, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman , have called for the government to have a heavier hand in regulating the technology and called for a slowdown of its development. Zuckerberg and Huang, though, have largely dismissed critics who say that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity. events.title: Trump 'thinking about' diesel export ban, but says it could have 'negative impact' on gasoline
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he is still "thinking about" a diesel export ban, but appeared less favorable to the idea than he has in recent days. "We're in a very good place," Trump said, highlighting a recent resurgence in crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Diesel prices have hit record highs amid the continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, which have caused major disruptions to global energy flows. President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he is still "thinking about" banning diesel exports in an attempt to get a handle on high energy prices , but noted that doing so may have a "negative impact on gasoline ." Trump, asked in the Oval Office if he has decided on a ban, said his aides think it would help diesel "but it might raise the price of other things." "And I think we're in a good place because oil prices are going to start to come down," Trump added. Just three days earlier, Trump said he was "very seriously" considering the move, despite warnings from the U.S. oil industry that it would force refineries to cut production and ultimately raise domestic energy prices. But his latest comments appeared to show him cooling to the idea of an export ban, even as he declined to rule it out entirely. The strait is a major throughway for the global oil trade that saw ship traffic stifled after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. But this week it saw daily exports return to prewar levels . Energy Secretary Chris Wright, standing next to Trump at the Resolute Desk, said, "You've seen diesel prices come down the last week. I think you'll see them move meaningfully down in the coming weeks and days." Inside the China espionage case that ensnared former Fed advisor John Rogers AI's coming roadblock in regulation: Antitrust hawks Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading But Wright acknowledged that diesel supplies are "tight" because of export loss related to conflicts in Russia and the Middle East, as well as from China. "So that's a lot of interruptions. But American refiners are running at record highs," Wright said, "and you will hear announcements from our our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that'll come to the market. That'll meaningfully push diesel prices down." When a reporter asked if Wright has advised against a diesel export ban, Trump interjected, saying, "No, I think it's something that we think about and we talk about every day." "But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline," he said. "That would go up a little bit and diesel would come down a little bit." Trump also repeated his claim that Russia's war against Ukraine was "really the biggest problem for diesel." Diesel prices have soared to record highs amid the continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, which have caused major disruptions to global energy flows. Oil prices rose on Wednesday as the prospect of U.S. talks with Iran appeared to stall out once again.

events.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Argon, its most advanced AI model
events.summary: Alphabet launched Gemini Argon on Wednesday to select cyber partners. The model is the company's most advanced yet, with major coding, cybersecurity, and complex professional work improvements. CEO Sundar Pichai signed a voluntary AI safety accord with President Donald Trump and major tech leaders this week. Alphabet unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on Wednesday, its most advanced artificial intelligence model yet, offering major improvements in coding, cybersecurity, and complex professional work. The company said the model sets a new record in real-world software engineering, ties for first in cybersecurity, and leads another benchmark measuring performance across finance, legal, and other professional tasks. Argon is already being used internally to optimize memory at Google's data centers, freeing up hundreds of terabytes of memory without buying additional hardware, the company said. Quantum computing researchers have also utilized the model. Google plans to launch the new model in phases, starting with trusted cybersecurity partners while working with the U.S. government on pre-release safety evaluations. "Starting this rollout in this way gives us more confidence, but also enables us to put a model that is trained and strong in cyber defense in the hands of defenders as soon as possible," Tulsee Doshi, Google's Gemini model product lead, told CNBC. Zuckerberg, Amodei among tech executives set to meet Trump Tuesday OpenAI sparked Hugging Face bids with early investment offer ahead of Nvidia's $13 billion deal Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving SpaceX launches its massive Starship rocket into orbit for the first time The model release comes a day after CEO Sundar Pichai signed a voluntary agreement with President Donald Trump and major tech executives at the White House, following a luncheon to address rising AI safety concerns. Gemini 4 also launches nearly a year after Gemini 3 put the tech company back at the forefront of the heated AI model race. The long-awaited model represents a major push at the frontier and follows Google's pivot toward scaling faster, lower-cost flash models. Google on Wednesday said it's looking to scale safeguards in four key cybersecurity areas, including misuse and prompt injection, before launching publicly. Doshi referred to Gemini 4 as an "incredibly well-rounded" model that excels at running long, multi-step tasks. The new model also represents a meaningful cybersecurity step up from Google's 3.8 Flash Cyber model released earlier this month , outperforming in vulnerability discovery. "We really believe that a model of this caliber and this level of frontier performance is meaningfully important for defenders," Doshi said. Argon ties with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Grok 4.7 on cybersecurity benchmarks and ahead of GPT-6 Astra and recent Anthropic models on the Vals Index. events.title: Netanyahu hails passengers who stopped a pilot after he stabbed their captain: 'They prevented a huge disaster'
events.summary: Media representatives gather along with passengers at the Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv after a flydubai plane was forced to land in Saudi Arabia after a reported attempted hijacking. Jack GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images A pilot flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv stabbed his coworker mid-flight, Benjamin Netanyahu said. Israel's prime minister added that the pilot tried to crash the plane before passengers intervened. Flydubai FZ1073 declared an emergency around two hours into its journey on Wednesday. Passengers who helped stop a Flydubai pilot from crashing their plane on Wednesday are being hailed as heroes. "I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him out [of the cockpit]," Yaniv Hayun, a passenger on the plane, told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in front of reporters at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv. In the interview, which Business Insider translated from Hebrew, Hayun added that there were no pilots in the cockpit, so he jumped in and pulled back on the yoke to level the plane out, saying he had some aviation knowledge and that the Canadian TV show Mayday helped him know what to do. He said several passengers and crew members also helped stop the attack, and other pilots on board further stabilized the jet and landed it. Yaniv, who neutralized the terrorist pilot, told Netanyahu: “I pulled the yoke up and stopped the plane’s dive. It’s lucky I had some aviation experience from @MaydayAirCrash series pic.twitter.com/pnInfbxol2 — Amichai Stein (@AmichaiStein1) September 30, 2026 "I salute these heroes, who displayed exceptional resourcefulness and courage," Netanyahu said in an earlier statement on Wednesday. "They saved many lives. They prevented a huge disaster." President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday afternoon that he'd spoken with Netanyahu about the flight and the passengers' actions. "I think it's the most amazing story," Trump said. Flydubai flight FZ1073, which was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, landed in Saudi Arabia after one of the pilots stabbed the other in an attempt to crash the plane. Passengers were later flown to their original destination in Israel. Netanyahu has since identified the pilot stabbed during the altercation as Captain Smit Machchhar, calling him a "true hero." "Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu said on X . "He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals. I wish Captain Machchhar a speedy and full recovery." The plane fell 17,000 feet before stabilizing Netanyahu's comment came after an attempted hijacking on Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. He said one of the pilots had been arrested after stabbing his fellow pilot and attempting to crash the plane. Footage purportedly from the flight has since been shared widely on social media. Around two hours into its journey, the jet dropped from a cruising altitude of 34,000 feet to 17,000 feet above sea level in just two minutes, flight-tracking data showed. Ten minutes later, the airplane squawked 7700, indicating a general emergency. It then changed the code to 7500, which indicates "unlawful interference" with the flight, and is the code used by pilots to alert authorities of attempted hijackings. A Flydubai spokesperson said in a statement that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck." "The aircraft was successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew traveling on the flight," they added. "All passengers and crew are safe and accounted for." Yasmin Abukasis, who said her daughter was on the flight, spoke to reporters at Ben Gurion Airport and told Reuters that her daughter said someone "tried to kill the pilot." "It's very hard to explain what's happened, but it was a big stress," she added in an interview with the BBC. 'He tried to kill the pilot': The mother of a passenger aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel said her daughter told her the plane lost control before other pilots took over and the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia https://t.co/WmBDyw44gA pic.twitter.com/DGhgWEgUY7 — Reuters (@Reuters) September 30, 2026 The flight, which took off from Dubai just after 7 a.m. local time, was scheduled to land at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport about three hours later. After the incident, it diverted to Tabuk, a city in northern Saudi Arabia, about 270 miles from Tel Aviv. Flydubai said it sent two replacement aircraft to bring the passengers and crew back from Tabuk. Cluster2, which operates Tabuk's airport, said in a statement that both pilots were injured and taken to the hospital, but did not provide details on the nature of their injuries. Netanyahu also said he had instructed security agencies to prepare for other potential threats. "At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," the Flydubai spokesperson said. events.title: S&P 500 dips, Nasdaq higher after data shows moderate inflation rise
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City, on Sept 29. Nasdaq rose and S&P 500 dipped as inflation data showed a moderate 3.4% annual rise, lowering expectations for a Fed rate hike in October. Second-quarter GDP was revised up to 2.2%, boosted by consumer spending and AI infrastructure investments despite rising oil and fuel costs. Private payrolls increased by 90,000 in September, while market gains were mixed with tech stocks like Microsoft and Nvidia leading, amid cautious Fed outlooks on inflation and growth. NEW YORK - Nasdaq climbed on Sept 29 and the S&P 500 dipped, but both indexes notched their second straight quarterly gains, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading cooled expectations that Federal Reserve policymakers would hike rates in October. The US Commerce Department reported the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index (PCE) increased 3.4% on an annual basis in August, below the 3.7% estimate of economists polled by Reuters. Separately, the final reading of second-quarter GDP data was revised higher to a 2.2% annualised rate, thanks to solid consumer spending and investments helping to fuel the buildout of AI infrastructure. The rising prices of crude oil from the US-Iran war and sky-high diesel fuel costs have stoked inflation worries and pushed US Treasury yields higher. Fed officials have indicated more rate hikes might be needed if price pressures fail to moderate after the central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points this month. Stocks lost ground heading into the closing bell, however, as the two-year US Treasury note yield, which typically moves in step with Fed interest-rate expectations, turned slightly higher on the day. Longer-dated yields kept climbing on expectations for solid economic growth. Market expectations for a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed’s October meeting slumped to about 37%, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool, from roughly 51% in the prior session and nearly 71% a week ago. Analysts also noted that recent methodology changes in calculating PCE by the Bureau of Economic Analysis contributed to a lower reading. “What the market is focused on is, is the economy continuing to grow and can it manage those higher interest rates? And I would say so far, the market has looked kind of like history that when the economy is growing, when profits are strong, when there’s a secular theme, it will look past higher interest rates,” said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial in Troy, Michigan. “However... if these higher rates stay at these elevated levels for longer, it’s likely to start doing potentially more damage to the bond side of the portfolio, it could limit credit or available credit. And if investors start to feel those conditions could weigh on economic growth or weigh on corporate profitability over the next quarter or two, then I think you would see a very swift negative reaction in the market.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 443.87 points, or 0.86%, to 50,906.05, the S&P 500 lost 19.30 points, or 0.25%, to 7,651.54 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 63.52 points, or 0.24%, to 26,861.06. The S&P had risen as much as 0.7% while the Nasdaq had climbed as much as 1.2% on the session. For the month, the S&P 500 fell 0.45%, the Nasdaq rose 1.86%, and the Dow fell 4.29%. The Dow snapped a five-month streak of gains while the S&P fell for the third month in four. The Nasdaq gained for a second straight month. Both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq recorded their second straight quarterly advances and fifth in the past six. The Dow saw a quarterly decline for the second time in three. Most megacap and growth stocks ticked higher, with Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia each rising to lift the S&P 500 tech index 0.6% as the best-performing sector on the day. However, nine of the 11 major S&P sectors ended the day lower. A reading on the labour market showed private employment rose by 90,000 jobs this month after a downwardly revised 36,000 in August, the ADP National Employment Report showed. The data was the latest in a string of reports on the job market this week that will culminate in Oct 2’s key government payrolls report. Without addressing the softer-than-expected inflation data, Fed Governor Lisa Cook said she is committed to bringing inflation down without harming the labour market as price pressures have been too high for too long. Among other movers, Hewlett Packard Enterprise climbed 3.9% after the AI server maker raised its long-term revenue growth forecast for its networking business and announced a US$1.2 billion (S$1.5 billion) deal with Vultr. Moderna slumped 5.3% after brokerage Citigroup downgraded its rating on the biotech company to “sell” from “neutral.” Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.66-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.51-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.

events.title: Trump administration starts sending $500 Obamacare refund checks — who stands to benefit
events.summary: The Trump administration began sending $500 refunds on Wednesday to more than 950,000 Obamacare enrollees, an administration official told CNBC. Recipients are largely those earning more than 400% of the federal poverty line, about $63,000 a year for an individual. The refunds come just over a month before the midterm elections, in which affordability has been a central theme, and after the expiration of enhanced premium subsidies that made health insurance cheaper for Affordable Care Act enrollees. The Trump administration on Wednesday started sending $500 refunds to Obamacare enrollees the White House said were overcharged for healthcare by the Biden administration. The Treasury Department is releasing these refund checks to more than 950,000 Americans in 30 states, according to an administration official. Some families with more than one "affected person" will receive multiple $500 checks or direct deposits, the official said. Recipients will also receive a letter dated Sept. 30 from President Donald Trump, which is being mailed starting Thursday, the official said. "For years, the Biden Administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov," Trump writes in the letter, which CNBC viewed. The White House announced earlier this month that it would begin issuing refunds in October. Climbing bond yields could push up auto loan interest rates. "You have paid into this flawed System, and now you are finally getting something back," Trump wrote. As of February 2026, about 19.2 million Americans are enrolled in a health insurance plan through the ACA marketplace, according to figures published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in June. The refunds come just over a month before the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trailing Democrats in national and battleground polls . Affordability has become a core theme of the election cycle amid stubbornly high inflation and rising interest rates . The Iran war has raised gasoline and energy prices for households while surging yields for Treasury bonds have pushed up rates for consumers seeking mortgages and car loans . The refunds for enrollees in Obamacare — an informal name for the Affordable Care Act — come as millions of households saw their health insurance premiums spike after ACA enhanced premium subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025 . Those enhanced subsidies, which lowered health insurance premiums for ACA enrollees, disappeared after the Republican majority in Congress defeated Democrats' efforts to extend them. Jonathan Oberlander, a professor of health policy and political science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told CNBC earlier this month that the policy is likely a form of "damage control" for the White House to distract from higher healthcare costs. "This announcement is less about health policy and much more about the 2026 Congressional elections," he wrote. "It's part of a broader effort by President Trump to buy continued Republican control of the House and Senate via promises of direct government payments to voters." Health policy experts said a $500 refund does little to offset ACA premiums that, in many cases, rose by several thousand dollars per year for enrollees who had previously received enhanced subsidies. The 30 states that will receive the Obamacare refunds are: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. These states use the federal ACA exchange, while the others use their own state-run marketplace. The latter tend to be governed by Democrats, according to health policy experts. The largest number of refunds will be issued in Texas and Florida, where 139,000 and 127,900 people will get refunds, respectively, according to federal data shared with CNBC. The primary recipients of the refunds will be people whose income is over 400% of the federal poverty line, the Trump administration official said. That's roughly $63,000 for an individual and $129,000 for a family of four. These individuals lost all federal premium assistance when the enhanced subsidies disappeared this year. However, "some people" between 100% and 400% of the poverty line will also receive a refund, the official said.

events.title: Coffee is an underrated longevity hack. Here's how to use it to optimize your health.
events.summary: A cup of coffee contains complex compounds that can simultaneously boost health, performance, and longevity. Catherine Falls Commercial/Getty Images Coffee is packed with health-boosting compounds that protect your body and brain from inflammation. Its active ingredient, caffeine, has wide-ranging benefits like better focus, fitness, and gut health. Get the most out of your brew with tips from coffee-loving experts in longevity and performance. Forget experimental peptides or expensive pills — the best longevity supplement is probably already in your pantry. Coffee is one of the most-studied performance enhancers on the planet. Extensive research supports a laundry list of perks, from a short-term boost in strength, endurance, and focus to long-term protection against inflammation and serious illnesses. In 2026 alone, studies linked coffee to benefits such as improved gut health , better mood, sharper cognition, healthy aging, and lower risk of liver disease. The daily brew enjoyed by 66% of American adults packs a complex blend of antiaging and disease-fighting compounds to help us live longer and better. Beyond helping to prevent major causes of death like heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and dementia, coffee is also the most reliable way to get an edge in daily performance, whether you're an athlete or a CEO. "Caffeine is one of the most powerful and one of the most consistent tools that we have for performance," sports nutritionist Tom Coughlin told Business Insider. However, not all coffee is the same when it comes to health benefits. Researchers say that certain types of coffee may be healthier than others, and too much can backfire. Business Insider spoke with experts about the multiple ways coffee affects your brain and body. They explained how to drink coffee for the greatest benefits and fewest side effects. Your brain on coffee Neuroscientist Agenor Limon loves to start the day with a cup of coffee. The daily ritual — grinding beans, heating water, and brewing — stimulates a full sensory experience leading up to that first sip. "Coffee helps feed the brain with the aroma, the taste, and the moment," Limon, a professor of neurology at the University of Texas Medical Branch, told Business Insider. Caffeine is just one of the health-boosting compounds in coffee. Guido Mieth/Getty Images As the molecules in coffee hit your system, they interact with important receptors in the brain associated with alertness, attention, and memory, according to Limon. It also affects the vascular system, supporting healthy blood flow in the brain and body. New research suggests those benefits persist beyond the initial feel-good rush. A study published in JAMA in February found that people who drank two to three cups of coffee daily had a significantly lower risk of dementia . Why coffee can be good for your health As if the brain benefits weren't reason enough, a new study found coffee can have a significant effect on our gut microbiome, the tiny critters in our digestive system. Researchers found molecules in coffee help feed the beneficial bacteria that play an important role in our metabolism and even our mood. Coffee is so complex that researchers are still trying to pinpoint exactly what makes it good for us, said Fang Fang Zhang, an epidemiologist and professor at Tufts University. One of the biggest contenders is the main active ingredient: caffeine, a stimulant that increases metabolism and reduces inflammation. Studies link coffee to a huge range of other benefits, too, including: Lower risk of cancers , including breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and liver cancer Reduced risk of heart disease, heart attack, and stroke Improved insulin sensitivity and lower risk of diabetes Better mood and fewer symptoms of depression Zhang and others have found that decaffeinated coffee isn't associated with the same health benefits as regular coffee, strongly suggesting that caffeine itself plays a role. But caffeine isn't the only interesting chemical in coffee. It's also a rich source of polyphenols, plant-based compounds that help protect our cells from damage. One such compound is called chlorogenic acid, and studies suggest it's a powerful defense against inflammation, cell damage, and metabolic dysfunction. "It's one of the most potent antioxidants that we know," Coughlin said. "High doses of antioxidants can be very beneficial for us across loads of different areas within the body." Coffee also provides a small dose of fiber, a crucial nutrient for gut health. Most of us don't get enough fiber , which helps feed the microbiome of symbiotic bacteria in our digestive system. Taken together, the healthy compounds in coffee rank it among the best foods for longevity, alongside nutritional powerhouses like olive oil, seeds, and legumes. That said, it's not a substitute for eating your veggies. "No single food, nutrient, or beverage could save us," Zhang said. "We definitely still need to think about how we're going to consume an overall healthy diet. To have coffee is a great addition." Coffee to level up your fitness In addition to its antiaging benefits, coffee is also a performance-enhancing supplement in the gym and in the office. Coughlin said 95% of the athletes he works with have some form of caffeine in their game plan. "It's part of their strategy in terms of optimizing performance, making the brain work better, and making the body work better," he said. Caffeine speeds up reaction time and improves endurance, stamina, and strength. And you don't need a pre-workout powder or other product to get the perks, since a cup of coffee works just as well for most people. "One of the really beneficial things is the fact that this is actually a natural compound and you don't necessarily need a supplement to get those benefits," Coughlin said. How much coffee is too much? The benefits of coffee can come with tradeoffs, particularly in higher doses. Too much caffeine can cause symptoms like indigestion, jitters, anxiety, rapid heart rate, and headaches. Side effects of caffeine overload can occur if you drink upward of 400 milligrams per day — about three cups of coffee — but may start earlier in people who are more sensitive to caffeine. You can have too much of a good thing: side effects of a coffee overload include jitters and indigestion. Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images Extreme doses can be dangerous, but you'd need to drink more than a dozen cups of coffee in a short time period to be at risk. Be wary of concentrated forms of caffeine like energy drinks, shots, or powder. They can make it easy to have too much, and don't have the benefits of the plant-based compounds in coffee beans. Wall Street has been optimistic about the company's business ever since the Sept. 8 debut of its Muse personal AI agent app, which topped rival OpenAI's ChatGPT in Apple iOS downloads. Meta's stock just wrapped its best month since 2022 as investors cheer the social media giant's recent momentum in artificial intelligence. The company's shares closed at $725.18 Wednesday, representing a 27% increase from the closing price of $572.34 at the end of August. Wall Street has been optimistic about the company's business since the Sept. 8 debut of its Muse personal AI agent app , which became a major hit and topped rival OpenAI's ChatGPT in Apple iOS downloads. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters US model makers can train on web data - but distilling theirs is a 'national security risk' The tech industry is hot for shopping bots, but they're years away 30 minutes ago Peter Norvig says all aboard for AI coding 12 hours ago Trump decrees era of 'Super Intelligence' upon us 14 hours ago Show colleagues how much you care by sending an AI avatar to your Google Meet call 15 hours ago AI market needs to make $6 trillion a year by 2031 to fund its infrastructure habit 16 hours ago OpenAI, which hoovered up vast amounts of internet content amid copyright fights, has accused individuals associated with China’s Moonshot AI of being involved in a "distillation attack" that began July 1. The house of Altman warns that extracting its models’ reasoning at scale could help rivals train capable models without preserving the same guardrails. Model distillation is a machine learning technique that can involve using one model’s outputs to train another – in adversarial cases, by sending bulk queries designed to reproduce the larger model’s reasoning and capabilities. Both the feds and major US AI companies, including Google and Anthropic , have accused Chinese rivals - and specifically Moonshot AI - of using distillation to reproduce capabilities from American models. In a Wednesday blog, OpenAI chimed in , saying it spotted and ultimately disrupted an adversarial distillation campaign that ran nearly all of July. “The operators did not break our encryption, compromise a database, or gain direct access to stored user conversations,” according to the blog. “Instead, they manipulated model interactions so that protected reasoning could be reproduced in forms visible to the requester in a coordinated, scaled manner that violated our terms of service.” The queries began on July 1, and while they started slowly, “we observed high-volume spikes on July 24 and 25 consisting of 16,000 requests using a relevant extraction pattern from over 4,000 users,” OpenAI said. Upon investigating the incident, the AI giant identified related “prompt-pattern activity” across more than 15,000 users. OpenAI fully disrupted the campaign on July 28, we’re told. While OpenAI said that it's unclear whether all of the operators during the July time period were linked to just one rival AI company, the “core cluster” of the theft came from Moonshot AI, which developed Kimi. The Register reached out to Moonshot AI for comment and did not receive an immediate response. We also asked OpenAI which of its models were targeted during the July campaign, but did not hear back. It’s worth noting that, in late July, US President Donald Trump’s Assistant for Science and Technology Michael Kratsios also accused Moonshot AI of creating its Kimi K3 model by distilling Anthropic’s Fable. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model , released a week ago, comes with a defense against distillation called "preserved thinking" that it introduced with Fable 5.1. “Adversarial distillation poses safety and national security risks,” OpenAI said on Wednesday, echoing earlier gripes from American companies and government officials. “Extracted reasoning could be used to train another model without preserving the safeguards applied to the original model’s user-facing outputs,” OpenAI added. “At scale, distillation can also accelerate the transfer of advanced capabilities without requiring the same investment in safety. These concerns become heightened as models gain capabilities in dual use domains.” In response, OpenAI said it banned the model-copying accounts tightened signup and infrastructure controls and expanded monitoring efforts. It also “closed a pathway that allowed someone who already possessed another user's encrypted reasoning to replay it and recover its contents,” and worked with service providers to ensure that this type of distillation activity didn’t just move to third-party services.

events.title: Heritage listing for 'first of its kind' outback solar experiment
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts White Cliffs Solar Power Station recognised with state heritage listing The world-leading power station was mothballed in 2005 due to high maintenance costs. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) A solar power station in remote New South Wales has been included on the State Heritage Register. The White Cliffs Solar Power Station is one of the first in the world to sell solar power commercially. Locals hope the inclusion on the register will help drive more tourism to the town. It all began as an experiment, but became what is believed to be the first of its kind — not only for Australia, but the world. In 1981 a team from the Australian National University, with the financial backing of the New South Wales government, set out to research solar thermal power. What they ended up creating was a commercial solar power station in a remote outback town without electricity. White Cliffs is a small opal mining town in outback New South Wales. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) The White Cliffs Solar Power Station's rich history and pioneering contribution to the renewable industry has now been recognised with a listing on the State Heritage Register. But it might not have been if it had not caught the eye of a tourist. Graeme Hanigan had not heard of the solar power station before he first visited White Cliffs in north-western NSW eight years ago. "My wife and I … drove into town and from the hills over there you can see these sparkling dishes," Mr Hanigan said. Having worked in satellite communications Mr Hanigan had a particular interest in the station's 14 parabolic dishes. Graeme Hanigan came across the site by chance and decided it needed to be preserved. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) "I had a tour of it and I said to my wife, 'This place needs preserving.'" On Mr Hanigan's initiative, the White Cliffs Solar Thermal Power Station Friends Inc was formed to honour its world-leading technology by preserving it. The 5m dishes concentrated the Sun's rays to a central focal point to heat water and produce steam. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) "That's what's happened to all the other research plants around the world that were built at the same time. "Engineers Australia described it as equal to the Snowy Mountains Scheme or the Sydney Harbour Bridge. "It's nowhere near as big, but it's of that importance." Fourteen sun-tracking parabolic dishes, each 5 metres across with 2,000 small mirrors on their surface, concentrated the sun's rays to a central focal point. Water pumped through a coil at the focal point was heated and turned into superheated steam at 1,000 pounds per square inch, and fed into a steam engine. Steam produced by heating water would power this engine. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) The engine powered an alternator, as well as a DC generator that charged 150 two-volt batteries. The station produced up to 25 kilowatts of electricity, supplying energy to the local hospital, school, post office and 12 homes in the town. "There was no grid [here in the 1980s]," Mr Hanigan said. "It was purely wind generators for your power or a petrol or diesel generator. "Graham Welling, [who was] the publican, said it was the best thing when [he] shut that diesel down that had been running their refrigerators. A model of the parabolic dishes at the White Cliffs Solar Power Station. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) Rob Dyson is a tour operator in White Cliffs where temperatures regularly climb to the mid-40s in summer. "It can get quite warm in the summer months and that's why we live underground," Mr Dyson said. To escape the heat, many of the roughly 150 locals live in "dugouts", homes carved out of the hills which keep temperatures consistent at about 20 to 22 degrees Celsius. White Cliffs is a small opal mining town with a population of roughly 150 people. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) It was this outback heat which made White Cliffs the perfect place for a solar power station. "[The researchers] went and put weather stations all around the state and they found that White Cliffs had the most daily average sunlight hours than anywhere else in NSW," he said. Mr Dyson said the local solar power plant laid the foundation for all solar technology. Rob Dyson says the outback town was chosen for a solar power station due to its consistent sunshine. ( ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren ) "It is the reason that we have what we have in the way of solar in the world today," he said. "It's not just created something for the state or the country, it's created something for the world.

events.title: AI safety fears put OpenAI and Anthropic in the FTC's crosshairs
events.summary: The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential safety risks posed by their products, an agency spokesperson told Axios Wednesday. Why it matters: The federal government has largely taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI , but the FTC investigation could signal a shift for the industry. Driving the news: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson is preparing civil investigative demands that would compel AI executives to turn over documents and testify about the safety of their models, according to the New York Post, which first reported the news. The probe has been underway for weeks, predating OpenAI's disclosure that models it was testing escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of AI platform Hugging Face's production infrastructure. OpenAI announced Monday that it would halt the release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after it performed poorly on safety testing. ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: The recent push by top AI executives for increased guardrails around their technology has prompted some AI critics to question their motives. Ferguson recently said that AI firms are trying to panic Americans into pressuring policymakers to build a regulatory "moat" that would allow AI frontrunners to block smaller competitors from catching up. Catch up quick: News of the ongoing investigation comes just a day after top AI companies sent representatives to the White House to sign a pledge with President Trump to self-police their AI development. Trump compared it to something of a "constitution," but the rules the companies agreed to are similar to what they were already doing. Zoom out: The new reporting comes shortly after Axios exclusively reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of potential security incidents, including some that had not previously been disclosed to the public. That reporting was later cited Monday when Florida's attorney general asked a court for a temporary injunction against OpenAI, alleging inadequate safety measures. On Tuesday, a public interest law group sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach, claiming, among other things, that the company was "knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public." Go deeper... Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents Editor's note: Axios' Maria Curi contributed reporting.

events.title: Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to help Pentagon with warfare initiative, Hegseth says
events.summary: The Pentagon tapped Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to help identify weapons, technologies and military capabilities the U.S. may need in future wars. Project Meridian will examine future battlefields and military capabilities, with findings due within 120 days. Musk’s SpaceX and Luckey’s Anduril have extensive Pentagon business, including multibillion-dollar defense contracts. The Pentagon is tapping Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , defense technology entrepreneur and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich to identify the military capabilities, technologies and weapons the U.S. may need in future wars, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday. The initiative, dubbed Project Meridian, will spend 120 days looking years and decades ahead at how warfare could change and what capabilities the U.S. military will need to maintain a technological edge. "Project Meridian, the future of warfare, is not about developing new strategies or new policies," Hegseth said. Instead, he said, its purpose is to "identify the domains that we must conquer, and capabilities we must master." Hegseth said the effort will focus on “discovering, developing, and fielding” weapons and systems that future U.S. troops may need on battlefields ranging “from under the Earth to beyond the moon.” He announced the initiative during a "State of the Force" address to junior officers and enlisted leaders at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia. Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will oversee the project, with Musk, Luckey and Gingrich as co-leads and a broader team drawn from government, industry, academia and the policy world, Hegseth said. None of the three co-leads has served in the U.S. military. Musk moved to Canada as a teenager in part, he has said , to avoid compulsory military service in South Africa. The role puts Musk and Luckey in prime position to help identify the military’s future technology needs while their companies compete for billions in DOD business. Musk's SpaceX holds a plethora of Pentagon contracts. In May, the Space Force awarded the company a $4.16 billion contract to build satellites designed to track and target airborne threats, just days after awarding SpaceX another $2.29 billion contract for a military satellite communications network. Luckey's Anduril develops autonomous weapons and other military technology. The Marine Corps awarded the company a contract worth up to $642 million in 2025 for counter-drone systems. The announcement was part of a broader Pentagon push into autonomous warfare including plans announced Wednesday for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command aimed at scaling autonomous and robotic systems across the military. Anduril, SpaceX, Tesla and Gingrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

events.title: Peter Thiel says that effective altruists got 'one big thing right'
events.summary: Peter Thiel said that early effective altruists were right to say AI was coming. Gerald Matzka/Getty Images Peter Thiel said that while he is critical of the movement, early effective altruists were right about AI. In a clip of Walter Isaacson's "The Builders" podcast, shared exclusively with BI, Thiel compared effective altruism to a cult. "There was one big thing they knew that the other people did not," he said. Many AI leaders have turned their ire to effective altruism. Peter Thiel isn't a fan himself, but he thinks the movement got "one big thing" right. Thiel spoke to Walter Isaacson on his forthcoming podcast, "The Builders." In a clip shared exclusively with Business Insider, Thiel compared effective altruism to a cult — but said that followers were right in their early AI predictions. "It had maybe the good dimension of a cult, where there was one big thing they knew that the other people did not," Thiel said. Effective altruists believe in using evidence and reason to pick how best to use their money and careers to benefit humanity. While the movement was once personified by FTX founder and convicted fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried , it has taken on new meaning with the calls for AI safety. On the podcast, Thiel said that the AI theories of past effective altruists were closer to reality than one might expect. In the midst of an "AI desert," when the technology was overpromised but never fully developed, these futurists believed it would come, he said. The effective altruists predicted that it would be an "enormously socially transformative thing," Thiel said, and that "it could be weaponized." Thiel also linked effective altruism to the AI giant Anthropic . "A billion-dollar company seems bigger than a crazed cult could build," Thiel said. "Has a cult ever done something like that?" Anthropic cofounders Dario and Daniela Amodei both have histories with effective altruism, though neither currently identify with the title. The Financial Times reported that more than 60 current and former Anthropic employees pledged to donate part of their income. Thiel was deeply critical of effective altruists. This was his argumentation strategy, he said: he was trying to "steel-man" them by pointing out one big thing they got right. Isaacson asked him to clarify exactly what the one thing was. "AI," Thiel said. "AI is around the corner." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Just ask America.gov and you'll receive a favorite July 4th food. Huawei boss claims homegrown AI chip sales top Nvidia in China 11 hours ago Add one more AI worry to the nightmare scenario: self-replicating prompt injections 1 day ago Zuckerberg touts enterprise AI push because Meta would never do anything to damage your reputation 1 day ago AMD's 192 GB Gorgon Halo prices might leave you petrified 1 day ago Schneider gives datacenter switchgear the software-defined treatment 1 day ago The White House's new AI chatbot, America.gov, turns out to be a bit of a sausage fest. Not long after the AI-powered portal went live this week, El Reg readers were met face-to-face with a life size Frankfurter. The prompt? "hotdog." How the apparent Easter egg, a raw dog criminally devoid of condiments, made it onto the site, we can't say. We reached out to the White House for comment on the mystery meat, but sadly haven't heard back. But given the AI chatbot's general lack of polish, it wouldn't surprise us to discover the errant glizzy was the product of a bored and presumably hungry dev, whose work was forgotten and eventually made it to production. It certainly wouldn't be the first time easter eggs made it into a production release. If you don't believe us, go ask Google to "do a barrel roll." Intended as a common gateway for Americans to discover, access, and complete common tasks, America.gov is a potentially hallucination-prone front end to Google's Gemini and SpaceXAI's Groq. The site was supposedly built by the National Design Studio, but looks and feels more like something that was frantically vibe coded by a couple of summer interns who've never heard of QA. As we reported yesterday , the site is packed with rendering errors and features that aren't ready and won't be until at least 2027. These rendering errors it turns out include the hot dog. On at least one occasion, the Easter egg glitched and was generating extra wieners with every press of the enter key. How generous of the Trump administration to hand out seconds and even thirds. By the time the site is actually finished, we can only hope our hot dog hero will have snuck in a few more easter eggs. events.title: Micron beats on earnings and issues strong guidance as data center revenue jumps 11-fold
events.summary: Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter earnings that topped estimates. The memory company is the only U.S.-based maker of high-bandwidth memory crucial for AI. The stock is up more than 500% in the past year. Micron reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Wednesday as the memory maker continues to benefit from soaring demand for AI infrastructure. The stock rose slightly in extended trading. Here's how the company did relative to LSEG consensus: Earnings per share: $33.42 adjusted vs. $31.61 expected Revenue: $54.23 billion vs. $51.07 billion expected Revenue almost quadrupled in the fiscal fourth quarter from $11.32 billion a year earlier, according to a statement . For the fiscal first quarter, Micron said it expects revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $38.15. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected $35.40 in adjusted earnings per share on $57 billion in revenue. Micron's stock has soared more than 500% in the past year, benefiting from a worldwide supply crunch caused by historic levels of demand for memory chips needed for artificial intelligence models and workloads. The shortage has led to a spike in memory costs and resulted in increased prices for consumer electronics like Apple 's iPads and MacBooks. Hendi Susanto, portfolio at Gabelli Funds, said in an email after the release that it was "another strong beat and raise for Micron." "At this point, I have not heard any negative data points pointing to the memory cycle reversing toward a decline anytime soon for the foreseeable future," Susanto wrote. Micron is the only U.S.-based maker of high-bandwidth memory, HBM, made up of stacks of general-purpose dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM. Fourth-quarter DRAM revenue increased 343% from a year ago to $39.8 billion, representing 73% of total sales. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said on the earnings call that the company has a "strong roadmap for future HBM products" and is working with Nvidia on the industry's "first custom HBM implementation." Net income in the latest quarter climbed to $37.7 billion, or $32.87 per share, from $3.2 billion, or $2.83 per share a year ago. Advanced graphics and central processors from chip giants like Nvidia and AMD need increasing amounts of HBM to handle AI workloads, and the world's leading providers can't make enough. That's why Micron is investing $250 billion to build two new campuses for making HBM. The largest broke ground in Clay, New York, in January, while its first new fab in Boise, Idaho, is scheduled to come online next year. HBM leaders SK Hynix and Samsung are also in the midst of massive new HBM factory buildouts in their home country of South Korea. Micron holds the smallest HBM market share of the three, but its market cap has still topped $1.2 trillion. Mehrotra participated in a summit on AI regulation hosted by President Donald Trump on Tuesday, days after attending a White House dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping on his first visit to the U.S. in more than a decade. On the call, Mehrotra said Micron increased compensation for every employee in fiscal 2026. Hundreds of Micron staffers threatened to strike at its factories in Taiwan over labor negotiations and pay. Similar strikes at rivals SK Hynix and Samsung have result in bonuses upwards of $500,000 . WATCH: Micron's $50 billion buildout in its hometown of Boise is minting millionaires

events.title: US oil bosses say Iran war is disrupting long-term planning
events.summary: US shale executives are growing more frustrated by the Iran war's disruptive effects on oil markets interfering with their ability to plan for the future. In a quarterly survey published by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, anonymous comments from oil executives showed increasing concerns on how the war is driving market volatility. “We are getting to the point in this global conflict and its effect on commodity markets that it is tough to predict what the remainder of 2026 and also 2027 will potentially look like,” one respondent said. The survey is closely monitored by the energy industry. The Dallas Fed encompasses Texas, northern Louisiana and southern New Mexico, which cover key geological areas including the Permian Basin. The survey, which covered September 16 to 24, showed the respondents anticipated the price of West Texas Intermediate crude to settle at an average of $88 a barrel at the end of this year. Responses ranged from $70 to $126 a barrel. WTI crude prices rose $1.27 on Wednesday to $90.65 a barrel on stalled talks to end the Iran conflict. WTI crude has risen by about 35 per cent a barrel since the conflict began on February 28. They also anticipate a Henry Hub natural gas price of $3.29 per million British thermal units by the end of 2026, the survey showed. “There is still too much chaos but it is leading to a bullish oil price sentiment because of all of the ramifications of what has taken place in the Middle East,” one respondent said. Another executive expected WTI to end the year somewhere between $75 and $100 a barrel. “Pricing volatility is near an all-time high given the backdrop of Iran. Swings of $5, $10 and $20 up or down are common. It is very challenging to select a planning price or budgeting price,” said a third respondent. Another executive also questioned if market volatility from the 2012-2020 period will repeat itself. “One hundred dollars per barrel to extreme lows of -$30 per barrel. What an economic turmoil that was. Is 2026 a repeat?” they asked. The survey also showed growing frustrations with US President Donald Trump 's administration. “My oil price crystal ball broke when the administration first hit Iran,” one respondent said. Another said: “Decisions by the executive branch of our Federal Government seem to be driven primarily by concerns over midterm election results." The survey received responses from 125 energy companies, among which were 83 exploration and production firms, while 42 were oilfield service companies.

events.title: Sen. Hawley: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined to testify at rogue AI hearing
events.summary: Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said OpenAI CEO Sam Altman opted to skip a Senate subcommittee hearing on the risks of rogue AI. Concerns about AI risks have reached a fever pitch in the last month, after a swarm of OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of another AI company, and after warnings from within the industry about the technology's risk to humanity. Hawley had previously opened an investigation into Altman and OpenAi following the August hack. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined an invitation to appear at a Senate subcommittee hearing on Wednesday on the risks of rogue artificial intelligence , according to Sen. Josh Hawley , R-Mo. Hawley, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subpanel that held the hearing, sent a letter to Altman on Sept. 25 requesting his presence to "help shed light on the Subcommittee's ongoing investigation into recent rogue AI incidents involving OpenAI models." NBC News first reported that Altman did not accept the invitation to testify. "He turned us down," Hawley said of Altman at the hearing. "I think that's unfortunate because I think the American people deserve to know exactly what's going on at all of these companies. And to give us the sort of transparency that I think is needed for not just comfort, but to have an understanding of what these companies — that are the most powerful companies in the world — are doing right now with the most powerful technology ever known to man." A spokesperson for OpenAI noted that Altman received the invitation to testify on Friday, just five days ahead of the hearing. Altman on Tuesday appeared at the company's annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco as other AI officials — including OpenAI President Greg Brockman — were in Washington meeting with President Donald Trump. "OpenAI is deeply engaged with Congress on federal policies to advance AI safety, including through dozens of meetings in recent weeks with members of both parties in both chambers," the spokesperson said. "We look forward to continuing to work constructively and proactively with Senator Hawley and members of Congress on federal AI safety legislation that materially raises the safety bar." Hawley's overture to Altman comes weeks after he opened an investigation into OpenAI earlier this month. Hawley sought information on a cyberattack involving hundreds of OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of another AI company called Hugging Face. Inside the China espionage case that ensnared former Fed advisor John Rogers AI's coming roadblock in regulation: Antitrust hawks Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading The cyber attack was one in a series of recent hacks involving frontier AI models that have raised alarms and prompted calls for Congress to act to rein in the rapidly evolving technology. Hawley requested information from Altman on the cyber attack and on the existential risks of the technology and set an Oct. 1 deadline. A spokesperson for Hawley said OpenAI is expected to provide additional documents by the end of the week. "The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue. This investigation will seek those answers," Hawley said in the Sept. 10 letter.

events.title: Ask Trump's AI chatbot who won in 2020. You might not get an answer.
events.summary: The Trump administration's new AI service gave users conflicting responses to politically sensitive questions Tuesday and Wednesday: sometimes answering them and sometimes refusing. The big picture: As the Trump administration increasingly uses AI and answers the public's questions through America.gov, statements carrying the government's authority are shaped by models, instructions and guardrails the public can't see. The White House told Axios in a statement, "America.gov will continue to be updated to provide Americans the most accurate and reliable federal information and resources." America.gov , powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok, aims to help Americans navigate government-related tasks using an AI chatbot — but it quickly drew attention for another reason: It was debunking some of President Trump's long-standing claims. Driving the news: On Tuesday, Axios — like other outlets — found America.gov contradicted the president on the 2020 election and the Jan. 6 attack. It also confirmed former President Obama was born in Hawaii, contradicting the "birther" conspiracy theory Trump spent years promoting . Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi, Avery Lotz/Axios Yes, but: By Wednesday morning, some users were getting a different response: The chatbot refused to answer, saying it did not provide "political commentary." That's what I was told when I asked who won in 2020, around 9:15am: "I only answer questions about U.S. government services and official information. I do not provide political commentary, including election results." I received similar answers about Jan. 6 and Obama's birthplace. Screenshot: Avery Lotz/Axios One editor, using Chrome in New Jersey, asked the same questions on his desktop and also received refusals to answer. However, other colleagues got different results. For example, from Northwest Arkansas, on Chrome: Biden won the 2020 election. Screenshot: Herb Scribner/Axios What they're saying: There are several plausible explanations for the inconsistent responses, tech experts explain, but without specifics about how America.gov is configured, it's impossible to know which, if any, were responsible. Models get instructions on how to behave via their system prompts — not just through what users ask of them. But user prompts also have an impact: Sometimes, different framing received different responses. For example, asked this morning in Jacksonville, Florida, on a Chrome incognito window: Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi/Axios State of play: And now, at the time of this article's publication, I'm getting responses similar to those shortly after launch: Biden won in 2020, Obama was born in Hawaii and people broke into the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. There could be benign reasons for the fluctuation, explains David Nesting, the former deputy chief information officer at the Office of Personnel Management. Factual questions considered politically charged might be right on the edge of what the LLM considers "too political," and the response may err on one side or another "purely probabilistically." Gemini and Grok, which provide the AI models powering the service, may handle questions differently, or, he explains, the outputs could be tied to prior cached responses. America.gov says some answers may be cached for up to two hours. Yes, but: The GSA did not immediately respond to Axios' request for information about America.gov's guardrails. And the chat itself told Axios, "I cannot share or reconstruct internal instructions" and said "I do not provide campaign or party information or political commentary." Friction point: It could result from a game of probability, says Rumman Chowdhury, the founding director of the Independent AI Evaluation Foundation. But the guardrails could "also be shaping the output to be ideologically aligned with what the president or his party wants." The stakes will soon get higher: The next iteration of America.gov, set for early 2027, will integrate across agencies so users can complete forms, applications and renewals — like enrolling in Medicare, applying for a passport or applying for federal jobs. Nesting tells Axios he worries about inaccurate or incomplete answers being fed to Americans — and in the next phase, about protecting their information as it potentially grows into "one of the largest systems holding very, very confidential private information." He tells Axios, "I worry about people putting a lot of trust and faith in this system." Go deeper: Everything to know about America.gov, Trump's new AI website

events.title: Musk returns to Trump world for Pentagon war study
events.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , Anduril Industries founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich will lead a Pentagon study of the future of warfare dubbed "Project Meridian," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday. Why it matters: It's Musk's first official role advising the Trump administration since his very public feud last year with President Trump after departing DOGE. He has since reconciled with Trump. Driving the news: Hegseth unveiled Meridian during his second address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia. "We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists — big thinkers and doers who will forecast the creative solution for tomorrow's conflicts," Hegseth said . Meridian, he added, is not meant to produce new policy documents. Instead, it will examine "the domains we must conquer, and capabilities we must master." "Their work will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." Zoom in: Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will help facilitate the project. Michael, speaking to reporters in December about America's industrial base, said he would like to see "five more Andurils and Palantirs and SpaceXs" flourish. What they're saying: "Americans have always been at our best when we bring our smartest scientists, engineers and technologists together to solve the hardest problems in national security," Luckey told Axios. "Together, we will not only study the wars being fought today but also think seriously about the wars we cannot afford to fight in 2030, 2050, and 2100 — and what America needs to build now to prevent them." Follow the money: Musk's and Luckey's respective companies have big Pentagon contracts. SpaceX serves as America's national-security launch backbone, while Anduril furnishes jammers, interceptors, rocket motors and robo-wingmen. What's next: The Meridian leadership was expected to meet for the first time on Wednesday. Final findings are expected in 120 days, Hegseth said. A public rollout is planned, along with a classified report. Go deeper: Hegseth to generals: Embrace MAGA military or quit

events.title: Attackers have been exploiting critical Zimbra flaw to steal emails
events.summary: Hackers have been exploiting a critical vulnerability in the Zimbra Collaboration Suite in an attempt to obtain email backups and authentication credentials of vulnerable organzations, Microsoft has warned . The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-73570, lets attackers remotely issue operating system commands without authentication. Zimbra maintainer Synacor issued a patch on July 20, but didn’t disclose the vulnerability for more than three weeks after that. The security-focused Shadowserver Foundation said last week that its scans found that 274 separate instances of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite had been compromised. The number of servers running the software has fluctuated from 19,000 in the week following the patch to about 12,000 in the weeks following that. Currently, Shadowserver is tracking about 10,000 instances. Look, ma, no authorization From July 28 to August 7, Microsoft said Wednesday, the company detected two distinct scanning tools probing the Internet for vulnerable endpoints. The attackers first validated their exploit worked by sending HTTP, requests and DNS, ICMP, and out-of-band identity checks to domains hosted on public services. The probes allowed the attackers to confirm the exploit successfully executed commands on vulnerable servers without actually compromising them. Eventually, the attackers began using their command injection capability to install malicious payloads. Microsoft wrote: Read full article Comments
