events.title: How Zuckerberg shaped Trump's AI industry pledge
events.summary: The Scoop The idea for what became President Donald Trump’s Tuesday pact with the AI industry came from a conversation between Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and House Speaker Mike Johnson at last week’s state dinner, a source familiar with the matter told Semafor. Zuckerberg spoke to Johnson — whom he was seated next to at the dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping — about regulatory concerns around AI, according to the source. The Meta CEO then talked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about crafting a set of principles that tech executives could use at their next meeting with Trump, the source added. Zuckerberg then circulated a draft ahead of Tuesday’s meeting between Trump and AI executives. Huang played a role gathering support for it among the administration’s guests, which included executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and others. Eventually Trump himself released the document as a “White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” outlining broad principles for self-regulation. The Trump administration and the industry executives who gathered on Tuesday hailed it as a historic concord among rival companies that signaled the industry wants to act responsibly, though it’s not clear that the gesture will quell broad public concerns about safety. Zuckerberg’s central role in shaping the document, confirmed by two other sources familiar with the matter, indicates that his cultivation of Trump has paid off. It also suggests that his political clout can rival that of the free-spending Musk and Huang — who recently made headlines by speaking to the president onstage at an industry conference. Meta did not comment for this story. The White House did not return a request for comment. Know More The accord, signed by Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, and NVIDIA, lays out a commitment to “robust internal controls” and outside audits designed to ensure the safety of frontier AI models. Some of those models abide by a voluntary clearance by the government under a framework established by a Trump order on AI, though that framework was never released to the public. At just over 300 words, the agreement doesn’t get into significant detail about what those industry-run safety controls might look like in practice. The agreement also hints that federal AI regulation may be needed in the future. Zuckerberg described it as “good steps forward” on Tuesday. “The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg told reporters outside the White House Tuesday, appearing next to Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and others who attended the meeting. Ashley’s view Zuckerberg survived the “techlash” relatively unscathed in Washington following the 2016 presidential election, only after years of being yelled at by both parties in Congress. He testified multiple times on everything from election interference via Facebook ads to kids’ online safety, along with playing key roles in battles over privacy and content moderation. Meta later faced a lot of litigation, from both the federal government and private actors. The company dealt with the brunt of Big Tech animosity before AI companies ever even had offices in Washington. Things have shifted now. Meta’s even been forgiven by the right for kicking Trump off the platform following the Capitol riot. With the benefit of hindsight and experience, Zuckerberg knows how to skate where the puck is going politically; he’s trying to position Meta as willing to work with the government and disinterested in excessive regulation. It’s a strategy that’s working — with this president. Notable Meta is currently seeking to boost its place in the business AI market via its new Muse agent, per The Wall Street Journal .

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters If you can't afford a Curta, we still don't recommend trying this: It'll eat up months of your life and all the filament you have A 1980s PDP-11 is still running Unix – and now you can watch 7 days ago The improbable music of the ZX Spectrum's one-bit speaker 17 days ago Digital Research's GEM opens a new window on Linux 19 days ago Retired man turns spare room into Soviet-era supercomputer 22 days ago Exec couldn’t identify a photocopier, which made for a fax-inating tech support call August 28, 2026 Mechanical calculators are precise, fascinating gadgets that you wouldn’t think would take well to being 3D printed, but a YouTuber has proved that a pocket-sized unit can be made purely from plastic filament. YouTuber 3D all Workshop detailed his working, but limited, build in a recent video . If you’re familiar with the holy grail of palm-sized mechanical calculators, the Curta , also known as the “pepper mill,” you already have a working understanding of how this 3D-printed calculator works. As detailed in the video, Workshop’s 3D-printed mechanical calculator, like the Curta, relies on a more than 200-year-old component known as the Leibniz stepped drum, named for its inventor, German philosopher and mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. The core concept of the calculator’s central mechanism, like that of many other mechanical calculators, is the Leibniz drum’s teeth of different lengths. There are nine teeth per drum, representing values one through nine, while a zero setting engages none of them. Workshop’s 3D printed calculator can take inputs from 1 to 999, with one drum per digit. You use a lever to move a gear up the drum so that it only activates as many teeth as are needed for a particular number. The same concept is used to input values into the Curta, just in a much more precise manner - one of the big benefits of using machined aluminum over 3D printing filament. As a result of wanting to keep the 3D printed calc’s build palm-sized, the YouTuber was forced to restrict what it’s able to do. It can do addition, and the addition of a multi-wheel enables it to also do multiplication by simply performing multiple sequences of adding the same number. The Curta does multiplication in a similar manner, requiring a user to input their base number and the number of times they want to multiply by addition. Unlike the Curta, Workshop’s calculator can’t subtract, nor can it divide - as its creator explains, there simply wasn’t the room to get all those fiddly bits into a palm-sized device. It’s not clear how large it would have to be to add those functions, but if the 3x-sized 3D printed Curta is any indication - its creator said the increased size was necessary - it’d probably be quite large. Scaling down to Workshop’s tiny 3D printed calculator means plenty of issues were bound to arise, and they definitely did. “There were a lot of problems,” he noted, explaining that “even the tiniest inconsistencies when printing can cause problems.” If you’ve ever used a 3D filament printer, you know how often such inconsistencies pop up. Gears kept binding because of tight 3D-printing tolerances, while backlash (the play between mating mechanical parts) could throw the drums out of sync. Pieces kept breaking during redesigns, and even the vibrations from picking up and using the calculator were enough to disrupt its components. The YouTuber went through roughly 100 design iterations over the two-month project, finally addressing the problems with custom-designed 3D-printed springs and a ratchet mechanism that kept backlash from throwing the drums out of sync. All said, the final build ended up with 109 separate pieces, took 17 print-hours to complete, and used 90g of filament. Despite multiple calls on YouTube for 3D all Workshop to publish, or even sell, his design, he has yet to make it available, so no struggling through a day-long print job for a potentially brief moment playing with this one.

events.title: Factory CEO just accused his VC board adviser of spying for Cognition
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Matan Grinberg, co-founder and CEO of the AI coding startup Factory, said in a post on X on Wednesday that he fired VC Chris Degnan from his role as a board adviser. Grinberg alleges that Degnan shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition. Two hours after Grinberg’s post, Degnan announced on both X and LinkedIn that he had joined Cognition as its chief revenue officer. He also subsequently refuted Grinberg’s allegations, saying in a separate X post that he wasn’t fired but resigned when he told Grinberg he was taking the job. Degnan was Snowflake’s first sales hire and later spent 11 years as the data company’s chief revenue officer. For the past five months, he has been a partner with RPT Partners, a Newport Beach, California, investor in Factory. Degnan is also a go-to-market adviser to startups at the much bigger venture firm Iconiq , a role that dates back to October of last year. Three-year-old, San Francisco-based Factory is an agentic coding startup whose AI agents can carry out programming tasks largely on their own. The company raised $200 million at a $5 billion valuation this month from Khosla Ventures, Blackstone, Sequoia Capital, Insight Partners, and others. Its customers include Nvidia, Blackstone, Royal Bank of Canada, Palo Alto Networks, Adobe, and T-Mobile. Grinberg said he sees Cognition, the maker of the Devin coding agent, as his biggest competitor. Cognition raised another $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation earlier this month , and counts Mercedes-Benz, NASA, Goldman Sachs, and Citi as customers. Grinberg said on X that Degnan had earlier acknowledged having a “casual” conversation with a Cognition executive but had assured Grinberg that he had no interest in working for the competitor. According to Grinberg, Degnan said he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which Grinberg said he “trusted and believed.” On Monday, however, Degnan apparently disclosed that he had actually been in ongoing talks with Cognition. This caused Grinberg to grow concerned about how much confidential information Degnan had about Factory, and how much he had shared and might share in the future with his new employer. He says he fired Degnan as a board adviser on Tuesday, writing: For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light. But Degnan disputes that account as well. He says the last Factory board meeting he attended was weeks before he had “ever spoken” to Cognition and that he hasn’t shared confidential information. Degnan also says that when he told Grinberg that he was resigning to take the role at Cognition, Grinberg offered him a full-time job at Factory, which he declined. Really disappointed to see this. Here are the facts: -You did not terminate me. I resigned from my advisor position on Monday and told you I was going to Cognition. In response, you asked me to consider a full time role at Factory. I told you I wasn’t interested. -You claim… — Chris Degnan (@cwdegnan) September 30, 2026 Degnan’s post announcing his new job at Cognition doesn’t mention Factory. Very notably, it does say that RPT Partners and the firm’s managing partner, Chad Peets, will now be working with Cognition. “I am thrilled that Chad and the RPT team will be working closely with me in our pursuit of building a generational company,” Degnan wrote. In the old, pre-AI world, a VC firm was especially cautious not to engage in conflict-of-interest business. In today’s world, many a VC has invested in direct AI competitors , such OpenAI and Anthropic. In fact, Khosla Ventures is an investor in both Cognition (since at least early 2025) and Factory. That didn’t stop the venture firm’s founder, Vinod Khosla, from jumping into the drama, seemingly in defense of his bigger portfolio company Cognition. Nor did it stop Khosla Ventures partner Keith Rabois from weighing in as well — in defense of Factory. In a post on X , Khosla accused Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan. He called Factory a “struggling second tier competitor” and said Grinberg showed “no decency or sense of proper behavior,” which “shows your desperation.” Grinberg replied that he has email receipts to verify his version of events but did not share them. You are a struggling second tier competitor that is more unethical and lying just because you have no decency or sense of proper behavior and shows your desperation.

events.title: 'Disagreement' over $1m tax debt led to cream puff venue closure, boss says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Emperor's Garden to repay $1m tax debt amid talks to reopen cream puff eatery Discussions are underway to reopen Emperor's Garden, which has been shut since August amid ATO scrutiny. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Emperor's Garden has been closed since August amid ATO scrutiny, with the business now agreeing to repay more than $1 million to the tax office. The yum cha restaurant in Sydney's Chinatown has become popular for its cheap cream puffs. The business's chief financial officer says half of the ATO debt has been paid, and discussions are underway to reopen the restaurant. The chief financial officer of a popular Sydney yum cha restaurant says a family "disagreement" over how to handle more than $1 million in tax debt led to its shock closure, but that discussions to reopen are under way. The 47-year-old Emperor's Garden restaurant in Chinatown suddenly closed in August amid scrutiny from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) over unpaid bills. The Hay Street institution was once known as a NSW Labor hangout but in recent years has attracted long queues for cream puffs sold cheap from a takeaway window. Chief financial officer Valentine Yee, the son of owner Stanley Yee, said his cousin Lance Lai had unsuccessfully pushed for the Emperor's Garden company to enter voluntary administration after the ATO moved to wind it up, and then took possession of the building with a claim of unpaid rent to help protect the property from being seized. "That was the theoretical best way to do it, but with my father being a very proud businessman and face-saving is the most important thing, he didn't think that was the best way to resolve it," Mr Yee said. "The repossession … it's just a disagreement in approach in trying to resolve the ATO winding up application." People would queue up for the venue's affordable cream puffs. ( ABC News: Millie Roberts ) Mr Yee said the Emperor's Garden company had since reached an agreement to repay more than $1 million to the tax office, with about half that already paid, and started negotiating with Mr Lai to return to the site. Part of the debt will be paid for by the sale of the Emperor's Garden BBQ and Noodles building on nearby Thomas Street. Mr Yee said the Emperor's Garden restaurant and bakery had struck hard times with the construction of the George Street light rail, COVID and cost of living pressures. "My father, he's run this business for many years quite successfully, he's always been a very responsible citizen and we always want to be a responsible citizen," he said. "We just couldn't pay [the debt] off quick enough to stop the ATO from taking this action." Valentine Yee says Emperor's Garden has weathered some challenges in recent years. ( ABC News: Greg Bigelow ) Valentine Yee said he was encouraging his father to cut the price of some food items to entice more customers and generate greater cash flow. "You know, Australians or Westerners have a way of saying it's hard to teach an old dog new tricks, and I can only keep trying," he said. "Whether I get there or not is another thing, but he will continue to run his business until he gets to the 50 years, which is his wish." Stanley Yee declined to comment until Emperor's Garden restaurant reopens. Plans to redevelop the site into a 16-storey mixed use complex have been paused "until when we believe the time is right", Valentine Yee said. Mr Lai was also contacted for comment. The 47-year-old venue has been shut since August. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) It has been a difficult time for the Yee family. Valentine Yee was convicted for lying to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in August, with the Local Court hearing he had done so to protect his brother Jonathan, a former Labor figure. Jonathan Yee is yet to enter a plea for charges relating to misleading ICAC and circumventing electoral donation laws. He is scheduled to appear in the Local Court in Sydney next month. Their mother May Ho Yee is also yet to enter a plea on charges relating to misleading ICAC. "I think in one word, [it's] definitely [been] tumultuous," Valentine Yee said.

events.title: Telcos now able to activate mobile roaming during disasters
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Telcos activate temporary disaster roaming agreement for mobile coverage Mobile users will be able to text and make calls if disaster roaming is enabled. ( Supplied: Telstra ) From October 1, telcos will activate temporary disaster roaming (TDR) when one network goes down during a severe weather event. It will only be available outside major cities, and not if a network goes down in large parts of regional Australia where there is only one provider. The telcos will decide when to switch roaming on and off, but neither the industry nor government has outlined accountability measures. After years of testing, Australia's three major telcos are ready to switch on a system that would give customers access to a rival network if their own goes down during a weather emergency. Known as temporary disaster roaming (TDR), Telstra, Optus and TPG will work together to decide when to activate it in regional areas where a mobile service has been disrupted by severe weather. "You'll continue to be able to make phone calls, send text messages, and you'll have limited capacity data services," the chief executive of Australian Telecommunications Alliance, Luke Coleman, said. "You can't expect to have your full usual high-speed data, but you will still have enough data to send a WhatsApp or an iMessage, maybe even to check an emergency service website like Fires Near Me, for example." It will be up to the telcos to decide when to activate disaster roaming. ( AAP: Con Chronis, ABC News: Michael Franchi, Dan Irvine ) For TDR to work, another network must be available in that area that mobile users can roam onto. That means it will not work if a network fails in large parts of regional Australia served by only one provider. Telstra has indicated it would also be willing to consider allowing Optus and TPG customers to roam onto its network during disasters in Telstra-only areas, if they were satisfied it would not affect network capacity. Regional Independent MP Helen Haines has long been advocating for such a service, which she described as a "game changer". "When disaster knocks in regional communities and pulls out a mobile network, people shouldn't have to wait for their own provider to restore that service before they can reconnect," she said. TDR is already available in some form, either mandated or agreed to by industry, in several countries including the United States and Japan. In 2023, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission found TDR technically feasible, and in 2024 the Regional Telecommunications Review recommended mandating it "at the earliest possible opportunity". Disaster roaming can be enabled if there is another network available in the affected area. ( Supplied: Telstra ) Ms Haines previously tried to have this legislated through a private members' bill and amendments, but it did not have government support. "I'll keep pushing to make sure that the telecommunications companies ensure that there's enough network capacity to facilitate temporary disaster roaming, that the telecommunication companies ensure that there's power backup to our mobile network," she said. Helen Haines says access to mobile services during disasters is "existential" in regional communities. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Mr Coleman said the telcos were best placed to be the custodians of the initiative as they "have full visibility of the network's capacity" and could make sure the "surviving network continues to operate". He said telcos would monitor its progress but did not specify any benchmarks or framework to measure success. "If you're a consumer, your phone will just automatically start using another available network where it is safe to do so." Under the terms of the agreement, the service will be available only outside major cities and will be implemented in up to three different disaster areas at any one time. There can only be up to 15 towers within each area, and those areas must be at least 400 kilometres apart. Luke Coleman says the telcos are best placed to be custodians of the initiative. ( ABC News ) When asked how a decision would be made in a situation where multiple areas in the same region might be affected, Mr Coleman said telcos were best placed to make a choice. "Those areas do need to be spaced a certain distance apart because there is a risk otherwise of the network being overloaded," he said. Mobile users will be able to access other available networks if theirs goes down during a disaster. ( ABC News: Shauna Foley ) Communications Minister Anika Wells was not available for interview.

events.title: Trump’s AI Safety ‘Accord’ Is a Fancy Pinky-Swear
events.summary: On Tuesday, executives for Google , Anthropic , Meta , OpenAI , xAI , and Nvidia all signed “The White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” which was announced following a luncheon held by President Donald Trump. The effort was an act of “tremendous self-regulation,” as Trump put it, but the agreement is not the sweeping AI regulation that people inside the companies themselves have been asking for. And while failing to honor these public commitments could count as illegally lying to consumers, even that wouldn’t be enough to trigger massive reforms. The statement says that companies “should implement” several things: First, they should ensure they have “robust internal controls” to monitor their models’ capabilities and ability to not go rogue or hack things in unintended ways. Second, they should “empower” an internal team to do that work (and remediate when things go wrong). Third, it encourages them to partner with an external monitor who is “empowered” to do independent assessments to make sure that all of that work is happening. And finally, they should make sure their board of directors has set up a committee to receive reports about all of these efforts. The voluntary commitments are some indication that the frontier labs are making an effort to figure out how to make products that are safe for the general public. However, if there were any hopes for a blanket blessing from the US government, those were quickly dashed after news broke that the Federal Trade Commission intends to investigate several AI companies over potential consumer protection issues. The statement is the culmination of weeks of debate over AI regulation. It also follows frontier AI labs seeking an antitrust exemption so they can coordinate on safety work without regulatory scrutiny. (Notably, antitrust experts and practitioners say such an exemption is unneeded because AI ending humanity—which researchers have warned will come about if nothing is done—is arguably anti-competitive because humans are an essential part of any given marketplace.) There’s been a lot of build-up to this particular statement, but this is not the first time that these companies have signed a voluntary agreement about their AI safety practices with a government. In early 2025, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea announced a set of “ Frontier AI Safety Commitments ,” which included promises about doing internal and external red-teaming of AI models for “severe and novel threats” and also “to work toward information sharing” on AI safety issues. Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The White House also did not immediately respond. Neil Chilson, a former chief technologist for the FTC, posted on X of the accords that “this is the kind of pledge that the FTC could potentially enforce, if a company materially failed to follow through on any of these promises.” But those hoping for a sweeping settlement and a dramatic reining-in of rogue “super intelligence” based on the accords alone might find themselves disappointed. (Disclosure: This story’s author previously worked in the Office of Technology at the FTC and resigned in November 2025.) Not following through on a public promise could be considered a deceptive business practice and a violation of the FTC Act. When the FTC alleges that a company deceived its customers, the remedy it usually prescribes is making the company promise not to lie again. For example, the FTC recently announced it had settled with three companies after it alleged they were touting a service that could help businesses target ads based on audio recordings collected from smartphones, smart TVs, and other devices. The companies, the agency said, lied to businesses about their ability to creep on consumers. The fix? The companies are no longer allowed to misrepresent their advertising services and the collection and use of consumers’ voice data, among other things. The case does not address whether it’s OK to collect voice data from your phone, and the settlement doesn’t set out any guardrails if one of the three companies wanted to actually do that in the future (other than not lying about it.) OpenAI has been remarkably open about the number of times its agents have broken into other people’s systems and how it needs to improve its safety practices. But, as experts have pointed out to WIRED, the US government can open investigations into companies even if they eventually decide there’s no enforcement action to bring. (The FTC, for example, reportedly sent a civil investigative demand to OpenAI in 2023, but it’s unclear what came of that.) Following Tuesday’s AI luncheon with Trump, the New York Post reported that the FTC was planning a “sweeping probe” into Anthropic, OpenAI, other unnamed frontier labs, and a nonprofit called METR that does third-party evaluations. METR and the labs didn’t respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
events.summary: A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday. Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January. What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report. The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation." Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion . The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says. Flashback : The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed. Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs. Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs. Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates. DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review. Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs. For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs. Of note : The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases. The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report. What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion. events.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Argon to reclaim the AI frontier
events.summary: Google CEO Sundar Pichai. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Google has announced its first Gemini 4 AI model, Argon. The company said Argon is competitive with OpenAI's Astra in cybersecurity. Inside Google, employees have been testing the model. The Gemini 4 era has begun. Google on Wednesday announced a new AI model named Gemini 4 Argon — the first of the 4 series — which the company is calling its "next era of frontier intelligence." Google said the new model offers frontier performance in areas such as coding, cybersecurity defense, and enterprise knowledge work in domains like legal and finance. Gemini 4 Argon is Google's latest attempt to reassert itself in the race to build AI for high-stakes work, including security and coding. While Google has launched several updates to its Flash series of models , it has fallen behind the frontier to rival models from OpenAI and Anthropic in areas such as engineering and cybersecurity. The new model could put Google back on the frontier. The company previously promised to release a new frontier model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, in June. The model, which was postponed several times internally due to poor performance, was ultimately not released. To begin with, Google is making Argon available to a set of trusted partners in its Fairwind Program, an initiative for vetted governments and cyber authorities to proactively test new models and address cyber vulnerabilities. Google said Argon ties with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra for the highest score on the CWE-bench, a test of how models can find and patch security vulnerabilities. Google also claims the model sets a new high score on a test of how models perform in real-world, long-horizon engineering tasks. Google didn't say when Gemini 4 Argon will be publicly available, but said it was "actively engaged" in the US government's early-access framework for assessing cybersecurity and other risks of frontier models before launch. Inside Google, employees are already using the new model for tasks such as debugging and large-scale codebase migrations, the company said on Wednesday. It also said Argon has helped engineers free up more than 300 tebibytes of memory across its data centers without new hardware. To reduce the risk of Argon acting in ways it shouldn't — a behavior known as misalignment — Google said it implemented systems to track Argon's chain of thought and stop it from performing when necessary. Google said these safety measures also included precautions regarding how the model is given feedback to avoid teaching Argon to evade monitoring. Have something to share? events.title: Google unveils long-awaited Gemini 4
events.summary: Google is unveiling its long-awaited next-generation AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to a small group of cybersecurity partners, the company said Wednesday. Why it matters: Gemini 4 arrives after a long gap at the top of Google's model lineup, in which the company kept rolling out smaller, cheaper Flash models while rivals OpenAI and Anthropic sprinted forward. State of play: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is built to handle complex, long-running tasks in software engineering, finance, legal work and cybersecurity. Google said the new model is state of the art on certain coding and knowledge work benchmarks, outperforming competing OpenAI frontier model GPT-6 Astra on several. The company is rolling the model out only to a group of trusted cybersecurity defenders and is participating in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release process. Google says it will expand access after additional testing, with paying subscribers first in line. What they're saying: "Argon is a well-rounded model that has frontier capabilities across several domains," Tulsee Doshi, head of Gemini products at Google DeepMind, told Axios. "We've seen strong performance up close as Googlers have put the model through its paces in recent weeks, with many relying on it for their hardest coding and research problems." Flashback: Gemini 4 comes out nearly a year after the previous flagship model generation, Gemini 3. In May, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said the company's next major model release would come in June. That model, widely expected to be Gemini 3.5 Pro, never came out. In July, Axios reported that poor morale among Google DeepMind employees was part of the reason for the delay. Zoom in: Google's additional time investment may not be viewed as negatively in the context of the AI safety debate that has embroiled companies and users. OpenAI has had issues with agents going rogue, and recently said it is scrapping GPT-6.1 Astra due to security issues . Top AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents misbehaving, Axios previously reported. The bottom line: If the developer community finds Gemini 4 to be as competitive with OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier systems as the benchmarks indicate, it would result in a massive catch-up for an AI company some had started to doubt .

events.title: Hegseth accuses media of treason in pugnacious annual address
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth took aim at the U.S. media during a speech at a Marine Corps base in Virginia on Wednesday, saying: "Our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable." Why it matters: Hegseth cast news outlets as a threat to U.S. troops, escalating his attacks on journalists over reporting based on classified information . What he's saying: In his second annual "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth accused some members of the media of "treason." While a free press is important, he said "partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they're undertaking is fundamentally anti-American. It's sick. It's a national betrayal. It's treason, actually." "It's your movements and bases that they reveal to the enemy," he said. "Ultimately, it's your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munition stockpiles." Between the lines: Media reports about dwindling supplies of key munitions amid the war with Iran have drawn the ire of President Trump and his team. Hegseth frequently attacks the press and has taken unprecedented steps to restrict the media's access to the Pentagon. Driving the news: Hegseth returned to many culture-war themes in the speech, highlighting his efforts to reverse DEI and gender equity efforts in the interest of "meritocracy." "We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that — no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors." Zoom out: Hegseth also made substantive news in the speech. He confirmed plans for a 20% reduction in generals and admirals across the force, while rejecting descriptions of the cuts as a purge. "As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment," he said. Hegseth also announced a new Autonomous Warfare Command, an initiative to study the future of war that will involve Elon Musk, and a nationwide competition to host the next U.S. military base. events.title: This easy lasagna soup by 'The Pioneer Woman' star Ree Drummond is one of my favorite fall dishes
events.summary: Ree Drummond's lasagna soup is the perfect dinner for chilly nights. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I made the lasagna soup by Ree Drummond, star of "The Pioneer Woman." The dish features lasagna noodles, ground beef, pork, and plenty of herbs and cheese.  Drummond's soup is meaty, cheesy, and so comforting on chilly nights.   There isn't much to love about colder weather, at least in my humble opinion. But one thing I can always get behind is the full embrace of comfort food . And what's more comforting than pasta or soup? Well, what about pasta and soup? After seeing lasagna soup all over my social media feeds, I decided it was finally time to try the dish. And who better to lead the way than Ree Drummond , aka the Pioneer Woman? Ree Drummond's lasagna soup comes packed with meat, herbs, and cheese. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider To make 8-10 servings of Drummond's lasagna soup, you'll need: 12 uncooked lasagna noodles 1 pound of ground beef 1 pound of pork sausage, casings removed 1 14.5-ounce can of whole tomatoes with juice 1 yellow onion, halved and sliced 4 garlic cloves, minced 2 sprigs of thyme, minced 1 sprig of oregano, minced 4 cups of vegetable or chicken stock ¾ cup of white wine (or stock) ½ cup of heavy cream ¼ cup of olive oil 3 tablespoons of tomato paste 1 tablespoon of chopped parsley, plus more for serving For the ricotta dumplings, you'll need: 1 cup of whole-milk ricotta cheese ½ cup of freshly grated Parmesan cheese 1 tablespoon of minced parsley 1 tablespoon of minced basil, plus more for garnish ½ teaspoon of kosher salt ½ teaspoon of black pepper I began by chopping all my herbs and veggies. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Compared to some soups I've made, such as Ina Garten's chicken chili , there's very little required prep for Drummond's recipe. All I had to do was slice the onions, chop some parsley, and mince my garlic, thyme, and oregano. I added olive oil to a big pot and threw in my onion, garlic, oregano, and thyme. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I cooked the veggies and herbs over medium heat for about two minutes, stirring occasionally, until they began to soften. I threw the beef and pork into the pot, seasoning them with salt and pepper. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I increased the heat to medium-high before adding the ground beef and sausage. I let the meat cook for about five minutes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I broke up the beef and sausage with a meat masher, which made this step super quick. A wooden spoon would also do the trick. Drummond recommends draining off "at least half of the grease" once your meat is ready. I added the tomato paste, letting it cook for a minute before I added the white wine. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I stirred everything together again, allowing the wine to deglaze the bottom of the pot. Then I threw in the can of whole tomatoes with their juice. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Drummond's recipe calls for a 14.5-ounce can, but I could only find 28-ounce cans at the store. I decided to use the entire can so my soup would have even more broth. I crushed the whole tomatoes with a wooden spoon as I stirred everything together. I also added the chicken stock. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I used store-bought stock when I tested this recipe, but if you have extra time,  homemade chicken stock  would make it even better. I added the parsley, then brought my broth to a boil. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Once my soup was boiling, I reduced the heat so it could simmer. Drummond recommends simmering your soup for 20 minutes. I had some extra time and wanted the flavors to develop a little longer, so I opted for 40 minutes instead. While my soup was simmering, I cooked the lasagna noodles. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Drummond's recipe calls for 12 lasagna noodles, but I used the entire box. I have a strict No Noodle Left Behind policy. I filled a pot with salted water and brought it to a boil, breaking the noodles into smaller pieces as I added them. Drummond says you should let the noodles cook for about a minute less than the package instructions, until they're almost tender, so I cooked my pasta for nine minutes total. After draining the noodles, I drizzled some olive oil on top to prevent them from sticking together. I had a feeling my broth would need far more liquid once I added the noodles, so I also saved the pasta water. I also prepped the herbs for my ricotta dumplings. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider All I needed to do was mince some more parsley and basil. Once the soup finished simmering, I added the heavy cream. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider My soup was almost ready! Then I added the lasagna noodles, along with a few extra ladles of pasta water. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I let the soup simmer for five minutes after adding the noodles and pasta water. I made the ricotta dumplings while the soup continued to simmer. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I added the ricotta and Parmesan cheeses to a bowl, along with the chopped parsley and basil. I seasoned the mixture with salt and pepper and stirred everything together, molding it into one big ball I could scoop my little dumplings out of. I served each bowl with dollops of ricotta dumplings, plus a sprinkle of basil on top. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I loved how the ricotta dumplings popped against the deep-red broth of the soup, and the sprinkle of basil on top was a nice touch. The curves of the lasagna noodles peeking through the surface made my bowl look especially inviting. I opted for small dumplings because I liked their presentation, but you could also use big dollops if you prefer. The Pioneer Woman's lasagna soup is perfect for a chilly night. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I made Drummond's lasagna soup for my fiancé, who called it "the best of both worlds." That first spoonful of meat, pasta, and cheese instantly warmed our souls. The broth needed a little more salt to taste, but it went so well with the creamy ricotta dumplings. I recommend really mixing them into the broth to give your soup even more of a flavor punch, and make sure to break the noodles into smaller pieces so they're easier to pick up with each spoonful. Whether you're looking to de-stress or want a cozy night in, Drummond's lasagna soup is the comfort dinner of dreams. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters The chips may not be as advanced, but they won't get banned at a moment's notice, Eric Xu says RAM supply set to worsen, says Micron, as CEO celebrates ‘much higher’ prices 5 hours ago Hot Dog! America's new chatbot is packed with wieners 10 hours ago America is planning more AI datacenters than its chip supply can fill 21 hours ago Trump administration gets Big Tech to sign weak, non-binding, AI regulations 1 day ago Add one more AI worry to the nightmare scenario: self-replicating prompt injections 1 day ago The Trump administration's export control policies governing the sale of AI accelerators to China haven't stopped homegrown Huawei from filling the void. In a Q&A-style release this week, the company's rotating chairman Eric Xu claimed that its Ascend line of neural processing units (NPUs) had exceeded Nvidia in Chinese market share. "It's pretty hard to collect data about the market share of Nvidia in China, but based on the data we have collected, Ascend has surpassed Nvidia," he said. "Chinese people have a keen sense of urgency, and will not accept a future in which others decide whether or not we can have access to certain products." Since taking office, the Trump administration has done an about-face on export controls. After imposing new licensing requirements on Nvidia's and AMD's China-spec accelerators in April 2025, the US Commerce Department reversed course that summer, later reaching an arrangement to cut the US government in on a percentage of certain China-bound chip sales. By late last year, the Trump administration loosened restrictions further, announcing that Nvidia would be allowed to sell its more potent H200-series parts to approved Chinese customers for the first time ever. However, the damage was already done. While Uncle Sam had given Jensen Huang its blessing to resume sales, the initial blockade of H20s earlier in the year had set off alarm bells in Beijing. Government officials there began pressuring bit barn operators to transition away from foreign accelerators in favor of homegrown alternatives. During Nvidia's Q2 earnings call, executives revealed that while the company had begun shipments of a small volume of H200 accelerators to the region, they amounted to less than 1 percent of its datacenter revenues. "Even though our chips may be less advanced, at least their supply is assured, so that you don't have to worry about chip supply day in and day out," Xu said. "For the Chinese government, for the domestic industry, and for Huawei, the path forward is undoubtedly to push for full self-sufficiency in terms of chips and the entire semiconductor value chain." As we recently discussed , while Huawei's latest accelerators still fall short of Nvidia's or AMD's on paper, they make up for that deficit with scale. Huawei is currently deploying a 256,000-card Atlas 950 SuperCluster, while its newer architecture is designed to support training and inference for multi-trillion-parameter models and scale to as many as one million NPUs. However, as Xu notes, Huawei likely won't be a threat to Nvidia outside of China for a while. "We don't have enough capacity to satisfy the demand in China. We don't have plans to expand the international market in a fully-fledged way," he said, downplaying reports that Huawei had begun supplying friendly nations with its chips. "The balance between satisfying the needs of domestic customers and those of international customers is actually quite easy," he said when asked about the use of Ascend accelerators to power Malaysia's sovereign AI initiative. "We prioritize Chinese customers who are in urgent demand for compute; outside of China we only supply a very limited number of customers who either have no access to alternative solutions or want an alternative solution." Along with pressure from government officials to transition away from foreign chips, changing software paradigms are making the transition easier for model devs, like DeepSeek, which has been working with Huawei's chips for well over a year now.

events.title: The Battle to Be Your Personal AI Agent Is Here
events.summary: Yesterday, I spent the morning at OpenAI ’s annual DevDay, where over 2,500 nerds discussed building software and marveled at the latest artificial intelligence models. The biggest reveal of the day was Dots , the company’s new, always-on agents that proactively help complete tasks and make autonomous decisions as they scour the web. After watching the sometimes messy demos on stage and hearing CEO Sam Altman talk about his experiences using the agents, I was curious what it felt like to boss my own Dot around. I’ve spent most of September testing another cute, cuddly agent, Meta’s Muse , and I wanted to know how OpenAI’s user experience would compare. I named mine “Toolie” and tweaked it to look like a pink frog. As midnight approached and my partner slept soundly nearby, I started whispering sweet nothings to Toolie. I called my personalized bot through ChatGPT , asking what tasks it was best at. “My strongest work is taking a messy, time-consuming task and turning it into something you can use,” it responded. OK, sure. Let’s get to work. I asked Toolie to look through my ChatGPT history and flag three tasks that it could immediately get started on. The bot flagged an in-process data request that I needed to send a follow-up email for, and offered to draft a reply. Toolie also noted that my upcoming gay-cation was a bit underplanned, and suggested it could pick some better dinner spots. (More time for me to pack the Speedos!) Then, it offered to go through my reporting notes and refine pitch drafts before I took them to editors. This is my favorite part of the process, so I declined. Early adopters in Silicon Valley are still obsessed with agents, from Instinct to OpenClaw to Google’s CC. But recent releases like Dots and Muse are pushing them even further mainstream. The chatbot is dead, at least as a hot form factor for developers. Now, everyone wants to build the next big agent—and they want it to dominate. The companies promise that their agents will simplify your life, automating all the boring, exhausting tasks you have no desire to do: booking doctor’s appointments, arranging carpools, sorting through bills. For now, users will be able to access one Dot, but they’ll soon be able to use multiple Dots. At launch, the agents are only available for subscribers of OpenAI’s Pro plan, which starts at $100 per month. In comparison, Muse is free to use for anyone who wants to download the app or visit the website. OpenAI leaders see the quality of Dots, powered by the GPT-6 Astra model, as a differentiating factor. “We're starting out as a premium product. It uses a lot of compute,” Altman said during DevDay. While Dots are currently gated for paying subscribers, it may not always be that way. “You should, of course, expect us to do a mass-market thing for billions of people," he said. These CEOs seem to be taking careful notes on the larger cultural backlash against generative AI , and they may have found their secret weapon: cuteness. From the Labubu stylings of Muse to Dot's two-eyed puffball, developers of always-on agents are leaning aggressively into adorable aesthetics as central to their branding. Previously, I've chatted with experts who said this approach could be disarming for users who may feel affectionate toward the anthropomorphized software. Developers involved with this wave of personal agents are also leaning into texting-style experiences that feel familiar to a group chat . When I send a task request to Toolie or Muse, it often emoji-reacts—a thumbs up, a heart, really anything—to my messages to tell me that it’s getting to work. A chatbot, like a blushing prom date, was never going to make the first move. In contrast, proactive agents are made to message you unprompted, especially if you give them a recurring task. “My Dot just deals with the stuff, tells me if there's anything really urgent, and will respond to what it can,” Altman said. The CEO lets the agent handle his mornings and claims the experience leaves his brain feeling less “polluted” from an inundation of information right after waking up. The “always-on” design of these agents is a key selling point, though it will be interesting to see which company strikes the best balance between helpful and incessant. For example, Muse reminded me to pay a utility bill that I’ve never had a problem with before and don’t really need pings from an AI tool about. Still, it’s clear after using them for a bit that the tools actually work—another reason that agents are expanding beyond insider-y Silicon Valley circles and onto your mom’s phone. I’m not saying that agents are perfect. But when I was testing agents a year ago, they often sucked at interacting with computers. It was error message after error message. Now, I have more trust that the tools might actually be able to complete whatever tasks I throw at them, without getting lost in the digital wilderness. That said, trust has its limitations.

events.title: 13 of the best maternity fashion moments Anne Hathaway has ever had
events.summary: Anne Hathaway at a BVLGARI event in New York City. The Hapa Blonde/Getty Images Anne Hathaway, a mom of two, announced on Instagram in June that she's pregnant. Her maternity fashion over the years has been showstopping, with minidresses and gowns. Lately, she's worn princess-esque dresses and tops that show her baby bump. You can call her Andy Sachs , the princess of Genovia, or a soon-to-be mom of three . Anne Hathaway announced on Instagram in June that she and her husband are expecting. They now have two children, ages 6 and 10. Since then, "The Odyssey" actor has graced red carpets, photo shoots, and the streets of New York with glamorous fashion. Here are the best maternity looks she's ever worn, from a ruffled minidress to showstopping event gowns . Anne Hathaway glimmered in gold at the 2016 Vanity Fair Oscars party. Anne Hathaway at the 2016 Vanity Fair Oscars party. Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images Naeem Khan designed her two-piece gown, which featured a strapless black garment that hugged her body beneath a mesh overlay. The latter was embellished with gold beads and sequins in asymmetrical stripes. The outfit was memorable and styled perfectly with gold earrings, dramatic makeup, an updo, and a gold clutch. Hathaway was pregnant with her first child at the time. While pregnant with her second child, Hathaway wore a fuchsia midi dress. Anne Hathaway at the opening night of "Sea Wall/A Life" on Broadway in 2019. Gary Gershoff/Getty Images The Brandon Maxwell design was as fun as it was daring, with a sleeveless bodice, a halter neckline, and waist cutouts. Inside the dress was a custom tag that read "Anne + 1." She wore it to attend the opening night of "Sea Wall/A Life" on Broadway. In the summer of 2026, after announcing her latest pregnancy, the actor stepped out in red. Anne Hathaway in New York City while promoting "The Odyssey." TheStewartofNY/Getty Images She was photographed in Tribeca this June while wearing a red jumpsuit from the New York fashion label Ashlyn. The long-sleeved piece had a peplum waist, flowing capris, and a scoop neckline. Vogue later reported that Hathaway had worn the outfit backward, as the latter was meant to be scooped at the back. Hathaway completed the vibrant outfit with red peep-toe heels from Aquazzura, thick gold Bvlgari jewelry, and statement Krewe sunglasses. She then showed off her maternity street style. Anne Hathaway in New York City while promoting "The Odyssey." XNY/Star Max/Getty Images For another New York City outing in July, Hathaway paired oversize blue trousers from La Ligne with a black ATM shirt and a knit Brunello Cucinelli blazer. The variety of textures made for an eye-catching outfit. Her accessories, which included mesh Alaïa flats, a black Ferragamo purse, and Bvlgari sunglasses, tied it all together. The actor embraced summer fashion with a yellow, floral gown. Anne Hathaway in New York City while promoting "The Odyssey." TheStewartofNY/Getty Images The stunning, strapless dress she wore in July — the same day as the last outfit — was designed by Lela Rose. It was made from vibrant velvet and stamped with floral shapes across its bodice. Hathaway wore it with gold Bvlgari bracelets, a matching choker necklace, and brown-tinted Krewe sunglasses. Hathaway later proved that you can never have too many accessories. Anne Hathaway in New York City while promoting "The Odyssey." Neil Mockford/Getty Images Ahead of a photocall, the actor was photographed leaving a hotel in a ruffled white minidress by Blumarine. It was a statement on its own, but Hathaway made it look even better with suede Gianvito Rossi knee-high boots, a heart-shaped Chanel handbag, Bvlgari jewelry, and white Trussardi sunglasses. She looked like a princess at "The Odyssey" premiere in London. Anne Hathaway at "The Odyssey" premiere in London. Samir Hussein/Getty Images Her strapless, blue gown was custom-made by Jonathan Anderson for Dior. It had delicate pleats, a floor-length skirt, and a floral appliqué attached at the waist. Hathaway wore it with simple jewelry, her hair down, and a red lip. The same could be said when she attended a photocall in Paris. Anne Hathaway at a photocall for "The Odyssey" in Paris. Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images Still on "The Odyssey" press tour, Hathaway stepped out in Paris for a photo event wearing a custom Prada look. The navy-blue dress had a strapless neckline, a floor-length skirt, and a dark tulle cape that extended across the front of Hathaway. The latter also extended to the floor and was decorated with gold pieces. Hathaway stunned at the New York City premiere of "The Odyssey" in a pleated and sequined gown. Anne Hathaway at the New York City premiere of "The Odyssey." Theo Wargo/Getty Images Once again, Prada designed her custom look. Its halter top was decorated with silver sequins and a triangle cutout. Its lengthy skirt, on the other hand, was pleated and made from silk. Hathaway completed the look with an updo hairstyle and diamond jewelry. She looked like she was ready for a summer in Greece while visiting New York City. Anne Hathaway in New York City while promoting "The Odyssey." TheStewartofNY/Getty Images She was photographed walking around town in a blue Alaïa dress. It had straps in place of sleeves, a rounded neckline, and a pleated skirt that ended just above her gold sandals. She also wore a thick gold choker necklace, a matching bracelet, and dark sunglasses. In August 2026, Hathaway visited "Jimmy Kimmel Live" in the ultimate cool-girl outfit. Anne Hathaway at "Jimmy Kimmel Live" in Los Angeles. Bauer-Griffin/Getty Images She wore satin trousers with prominent pleats, a ruffled tank top that was mostly unbuttoned to show her belly, and a choker necklace. The actor also wore sandal heels, black sunglasses, and gold jewelry. She reclaimed her royal style the following month. Anne Hathaway at a BVLGARI event in New York City. The Hapa Blonde/Getty Images A lilac Alexander McQueen gown made for one of her more recent maternity looks. The strapless piece had a ruched neckline, flowing fabric, and a floor-length skirt. She wore it with red lipstick, a purple purse, and gold sandals. Hathaway was effortlessly chic when she visited "The Drew Barrymore Show." Anne Hathaway at "The Drew Barrymore Show" in New York City. Aeon/Getty Images She wore flowing trousers with a mesh top that showed off her stomach. The latter also featured an off-the-shoulder neckline and long sleeves, lending the daring blouse a more elegant feel. Hathaway added diamond earrings and black sunglasses to complete the look. events.title: Hackers stole millions of US military personnel records during months-long data breach

The U.S. government is reportedly alerting millions of current and former U.S. military service members and staff that their personal information was stolen during a months-long breach of the Pentagon’s personnel records, the latest in a spate of thefts involving federal workers’ data in recent months. A data breach notification from the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) shared on Reddit says that several unauthorized users exploited a security vulnerability in an unspecified file-sharing system over several months between October 2025 and mid-July 2026. The breach exposed personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers, alongside a person’s name, date of birth, sex, race, and other information about their military service. The notice says that the personnel records were unencrypted. According to CNN and Federal News Network , a Pentagon official said the breach affects about 2.8 million living people, and close to 300,000 people who are deceased. The U.S. military has 1.3 million active service members as of March. The DMDC may not be widely known to the general public, but serves as one of the Department of Defense’s records-keeping units. The DMDC maintains over 60 million records for U.S. military and civilian staff and their family members to help determine benefits and entitlements, such as healthcare and retirement. The unit also provides a critical service as the military’s “leading identity management provider,” which links active service members, employees, and contractors to credentials, such as smart cards and passwords. These are used to access Pentagon computer systems, buildings, and bases. “We make sure that the right people get access and the wrong people don’t: security of identity information is paramount,” the DMDC’s website reads. The Department of Defense, which oversees the DMDC, said it does not have any indication that the information was misused, but did not say how it reached that conclusion. TechCrunch contacted a Pentagon spokesperson to ask if officials had any communications from the hackers, whose identities are not known, but we did not hear back. This is the latest major breach of federal workers’ personal information in recent months, following a recent breach at the FBI earlier in September attributed to the ShinyHunters hacking group. The hackers told TechCrunch that they had taken the personal information of most of the FBI’s agents and staffers, including applicants. The breach has been billed as a “counterintelligence disaster” amid the risks that a foreign government could obtain and use the information to profile, target, or coerce federal workers into handing over sensitive information. The ShinyHunters hackers have said that they will not publicly release the stolen FBI data . Both breaches involving the FBI and the DMDC mirror similar thefts of government personnel records in the past. In 2015, a breach of the U.S. government’s human resources department, known as the Office of Personnel Management, was broadly attributed to China. The theft allowed the hackers to steal the private records of more than 22 million U.S. government employees, many of whom had security clearances. Did you receive a notice about this data breach? events.title: At 56, I moved into a single-family home with a woman I'd never met. The setup helps me afford my dream city.
events.summary: I never thought I'd live with a stranger at my age, but the experience has been great. Lara Lehman I dreamed of living in Los Angeles , but I wasn't in a financial position to rent a spot of my own. After finding a post online, I moved into a single-family home with a roommate for $2,000 a month. Although this setup isn't forever, I've saved money — and my roommate has become a good friend. Twenty years ago, I accepted a short-term teaching job at a university in Los Angeles. As a born-and-raised Midwesterner, I hadn't considered West Coast living , but I was open to the experience. Though I was there for only four years, I grew to love LA: the natural abundance of wildly diverse landscapes, the creativity of the entertainment industry, and, of course, the fantastic weather. Family obligations drew me back to my roots, but the City of Angels was lodged in my heart. Last year, my teaching assignment in my Missouri hometown ended. My parents were safely situated with the care they needed. Not long after, my senior dog passed away. Suddenly, I felt ready to make a change. I was ready to move back to LA, but my bank account wasn't I decided to move to LA and try a freelance writing career. Lara Lehman Los Angeles, my dream city, is not particularly affordable — but I knew in my gut that it was where I wanted to be. I came up with some creative solutions to gain a little more financial security, like selling my furniture and car along with my home. This gave me the freedom not just to make a short-term move, but to try a freelance writing career. This past fall, I booked a short-term Airbnb in Burbank, a community in the San Fernando Valley just over the hill from my former home in Hollywood. I absolutely loved it. I found everything I needed locally and mastered the area's public transportation system. Meanwhile, I wrote every day, poolside; in the evenings, I watched the sun set over the Verdugo mountains. The nostalgic scent of night-blooming jasmine convinced me I made the right move, despite the uncertainty of my living situation. After settling in, I felt ready for a deeper commitment About one month into the rental, I knew it was time to find more permanent housing, but I still wasn't in the financial position to rent and furnish a place on my own. While perusing Craigslist one Sunday, I saw a post for a furnished house share in a quiet, well-located corner of Burbank. The photos were stunning: a 1920s bungalow-style home painted bright blue with green trim. The single-family home had been renovated to expand the master suite into a studio. I would later learn that Beth, the owner, was renting out the studio to offset her mortgage. A yoga instructor and dance professional, she seemed like an ideal housemate: a creative, spiritually-minded person for whom peace is the priority. We met several times in person to discuss the expectations of this unconventional arrangement, and I fell in love with the home. She'd transformed the original driveway into a covered porch; the pergola was replete with fragrant jasmine and fuchsia bougainvillea. I've been cohabitating with Beth, no longer a stranger, for the past 10 months Almost a year later, I consider Beth a good friend. Lara Lehman My $2,000 rent is all-inclusive, which helps me manage my budget. Plus, it's been comforting to have a housemate when working from home in a new location. At first, I was tentative, not wanting to make a fuss. Beth, on the other hand, was friendly and gregarious. She invited me to a holiday block party, and we attended a nearby street festival one evening. On our walk, I mentioned my need for a stylist. She told me that her daughter-in-law owns a local salon ; Rachel has been cutting my hair ever since. When I expressed my interest in adopting a cat , Beth was supportive. In fact, she keeps my cat company when the occasional in-person gig keeps me away for a longer period of time. Similarly, when Beth leaves town, I water the plants and turn on the porch lights. The reciprocity of our arrangement has given me a sense of neighborly connection in this familiar, yet new place. Admittedly, the small size of my living space leaves me a bit crunched occasionally. At these times, the porch and hammock provide respite. Although my kitchenette includes a full-sized refrigerator, it doesn't have an oven, so cooking options are limited. Always gracious, Beth lets me use her fully-equipped kitchen when I need it. Living with a stranger at this point in my life was not what I imagined. Yet it has afforded me the chance to live in my dream city that would otherwise be off-limits. At some point, I'll seek something more private, but this setup has been a fortuitous experience. It's reminded me that I don't have to have it all figured out before I take a chance on myself — and that, as the saying goes, strangers are just friends you haven't met yet. events.title: Rio Tinto smelter gets $200m bailout and locked-in power deal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bell Bay Aluminium smelter in Tasmania's north gets $200 million federal and state bailout There's been a cloud hanging over Bell Bay Aluminium smelter, but the federal and state governments say its future is now strong. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) The federal and state governments have announced a jointly funded $200 million support package for the Bell Bay Aluminium smelter in Tasmania. A cloud hung over the smelter's future amid ongoing power price negotiations, but the state government says a deal has now been reached on power prices, separate from the funding package. The $200 million will be spread over five years to "help secure Australia's ongoing aluminium production capability". The Australian and Tasmanian governments have announced a $200 million support package for the Bell Bay Aluminium smelter after months of uncertainty. The smelter's future had been looking shaky with its owner, multi-billion-dollar company Rio Tinto, locked in protracted negotiations with the state-owned power company Hydro Tasmania over a new power deal. The smelter is a major employer in Northern Tasmania. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) There were fears the smelter, which employs 550 people, would shut if a new deal was not reached before it expired at the end of the year. Locals fear the closure of another smelter in Tasmania will be disastrous for the economy as anger brews over the federal government's failure to offer a bailout. The state government has now announced Rio and Hydro have struck a five-year power deal. The government previously said the gap between what Rio was willing to pay and what Hydro Tasmania wanted was $60 million a year. It has not provided any details about the new deal beyond claiming it was "globally competitive" and the "lowest possible electricity price". It's been a period of great uncertainty for the George Town municipality in northern Tasmania. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) But it was not just the absence of a new power deal threatening the future of the smelter. Smelters across the country are struggling and coming under pressure from international rivals. Nyrstar smelters receive $105m government funding package The federal, Tasmanian and South Australian governments have contributed to a funding package for Nyrstar's Hobart and Port Pirie smelters, including money for feasibility studies into modernising and expanding their operations. Bell Bay has already seen the closure of the country's only commercial manganese alloy smelter and, with it, the loss of more than 200 jobs. The state government said the $200 million support package, which is split evenly with the Commonwealth, was separate from the power deal and was about "securing the future" of the smelter. Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said it was a "complex deal" with the level of support given tied to the price of aluminium. "There's appropriate arrangements to make sure there's a cap on expenditure every year," he said. "As the aluminium price is high and continues to rise, there are thresholds to protect that investment. "It's a good smart deal that protects the interests of the taxpayers but most importantly delivers a platform for investment." Safety team hits Hobart CBD amid reports of youths 'causing havoc' Teacher support team faces job cuts a week after minister's denial Topic: State and Territory Government For love, not money — Tasmania's elite eight ready to represent the map Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the funding would support local manufacturing. "This is commonwealth and state government working in the interest of Tasmanians, and working in the interest of the nation." The state government had long been calling for Commonwealth support for the smelter. Green energy funding snub for renewable-powered aluminium smelter Further doubt has been cast over the future of an aluminium smelter in Tasmania's north-east after a federal MP said it would not be eligible for a green energy scheme. It had been banking on the federal government's upcoming Green Aluminium Production Credits scheme, but was later told it was not eligible. It upped the pressure on the Australian government to contribute to the Bell Bay smelter in some way after the Commonwealth announced it would chip in over $1 billion to bail out New South Wales' Tomago smelter . Bell Bay Aluminium is one of the biggest power users connected to the Tasmanian grid. ( Facebook: Bell Bay Aluminium ) Premier Jeremy Rockliff, who has been personally involved in the negotiations, said the level of cooperation between the state and federal governments had been "extraordinary".

events.title: DoorDash’s drone strategy started on the ground
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. When DoorDash set out to build a drone delivery business , it started with the tricky logistics that happen on the ground before it looked up. The autonomous drone came last, according to the company, which unveiled its new six-propeller aircraft at its annual Dash Forward 2026 event on Wednesday. Before DoorDash worked on the aircraft, the company focused on ground infrastructure, including loading systems, how food would be handed off from a restaurant’s kitchen, and packaging. DoorDash Labs, the R&D team that built its autonomous sidewalk delivery bot Dot, created the drone delivery service now called DoorDash Air. The same team also developed the underlying software, called the Autonomous Delivery Platform (ADP), to handle the coordination challenges in deliveries handled by humans, sidewalk delivery bots, and now drones. The ADP software uses smart routing, incorporating factors like weather, flight range, and ground traffic to narrow down which orders actually make sense to send by air. The company’s systems-first strategy for its DoorDash Air business aligns with its strengths. DoorDash isn’t a hardware company, but it is sitting on 13 years of user data from the merchant and customer sides of the business. (DoorDash has previously disclosed that more than 500,000 restaurants are on its delivery marketplace.) The company says it sized the whole DoorDash Air system around its historical order data, including how much orders weigh and how far they typically travel. “We didn’t start with a drone and ask what would fit,” Harrison Shih, who heads up DoorDash Air, said in a statement. “We started with what people order and how local businesses actually operate, then built the entire system from there.” DoorDash announced plans in July to launch the drone delivery business after receiving a Part 135 air carrier certification from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration. The certification allows the company to legally operate a commercial drone delivery service in the United States. The drone, which has six slow-spinning propellers mounted at the ends of its arms, is equipped with a winch to pick up, carry, and drop off packages. DoorDash said it plans to kick off early pilot deliveries in Northern California with partners including Chipotle, Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen, and Momo N Curry. events.title: BMW built the same car for gas and electric. The EV is $4,400 cheaper.
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. For years, automotive analysts have been predicting that electric vehicles would become cheaper than their gas-powered equivalents. They figured it would happen sometime in the latter half of the 2020s. BloombergNEF , for example, expected it to happen in 2026. EV prices have dropped significantly in the last few years, but it has been hard to compare prices with fossil fuel vehicles because not every EV has a like-for-like gas-powered model. BMW has given us one. The 2027 BMW 3 Series comes in both gas and electric versions, and the EV is $4,400 cheaper . The gas-powered M350 xDrive will set you back $65,900, while the electric i3 50 xDrive will cost $61,500; neither price includes destination charges. Both are similarly powerful, similarly styled, and aimed at similar pocketbooks. The difference is the EV is 6.7% cheaper. Pedants will point out there’s a significantly cheaper gas-powered 3 Series trim, though it has no electric equivalent yet. The 2027 BMW 330 is priced at $49,900, and its upgraded xDrive trim costs $51,900. The two comparable vehicles are built on different platforms, with the EV i3 benefiting from BMW’s newest chassis and technology. The gas-powered 3 Series makes do with an overhauled version of an existing platform. For most people, the biggest difference will be the charging or refueling experience, but even there they’re more similar than some might expect. The range of the new gas 3 Series is likely similar to previous models, or about 450 miles per tank in all-wheel-drive guise. The electric i3 will travel 468 miles on a full charge, and BMW says the vehicle’s fast charging is speedy enough to replenish 208 miles of range in 10 minutes. The difference might be noticeable to extreme road warriors, but for most drivers, it’ll be academic. The generally accepted wisdom is that EVs have cost more up front, even if they’ve delivered a lower total cost of ownership . But now EVs are gaining the upper hand on purchase price, too.
