events.title: I'm an American living in Europe. Here are 5 of my favorite cities to visit.
events.summary: As an American living in Europe, Barcelona is one of my favorite cities to visit. Emily Pogue I'm an American who moved to the Netherlands earlier this year. Although I've always loved traveling around Europe, I'm now able to do so with ease. Some of my favorite cities to explore include Salzburg, Budapest, and Barcelona. I've always loved traveling around Europe . But now that I moved from the US to the Netherlands, I have even more of an excuse to explore the continent. Over the years, I've checked 19 European countries off my bucket list. Here are five of my favorite cities to visit. Salzburg, Austria, offers a perfect mix of history and movie nostalgia. Emily Pogue I'll admit, I was originally pulled toward Salzburg, Austria, because I wanted to see the fountain from " The Sound of Music " (and it didn't disappoint). However, I found the city offers so much more. My husband and I stumbled upon Mozart's childhood home, explored the sprawling Fortress Hohensalzburg that towers over the city, and had a pretzel and beer at the Stiegl brewery. I wasn't quite done with my personal "The Sound of Music" tour, though, so we also visited the Felsenreitschule Amphitheatre — the stone venue where the von Trapp family sings in the film. It's also where the Salzburg Music Festival is hosted every summer. I learned so much during my time in Budapest. undefined undefined/Getty Images During my visit to Budapest, one of my favorite activities was exploring Margaret Island, a 1.6-mile-long stretch of land that has everything from swimming pools to an outdoor theater. After the sun went down, I loved visiting the Musical Fountain, where I caught a colorful water and light show complete with music. It looked like something straight out of the movie "Fantasia." I also recommend heading to some of the museums and memorials to learn more about some of the darker chapters in Budapest's history. These experiences were emotional but I learned a lot. For example, I held back tears while touring the House of Terror museum , which commemorates victims of Hungary's fascist and communist dictatorships. Visiting the haunting "Shoes on the Danube Bank" memorial — which honors the Jewish victims who were shot into the Danube by members of the Arrow Cross Party — was also a moving and worthwhile experience. Florence is the perfect Italian getaway. Emily Pogue I love Florence because, in my opinion, the city feels like a giant open-air museum. You turn one corner, and you're face-to-face with the iconic Duomo. Go a few more blocks and duck into an unassuming museum and you're greeted by Michelangelo's 17-foot-tall David statue. Although the art museums in Florence are unmatched, my favorite experience was grabbing a pistachio cannoli as big as my forearm, crossing the bridge to Piazzale Michelangelo, and soaking up the view under the warm Italian sun. Another great thing about Florence? Its proximity to the smaller Italian cities that are equally worth a visit, like Siena, Pisa, and Vinci. Meandering around Bath, England, makes me feel like Georgian royalty. Glowimages/Getty Images If I'm going to England, I'm going to make every effort to hop on a train to Bath. Walking around blocks filled with honey-colored limestone buildings really does feel like you've been transported into a Jane Austen novel. Despite being a smaller city, I've never had difficulty finding something to do. Of course, there's the tour of the beautifully preserved 2000-year-old Roman baths . Then there's my favorite spot in town: the Royal Crescent, a row of 30 terraced houses that has been featured in "Bridgerton" and several "Persuasion" adaptations. I particularly enjoyed touring the No. 1 Royal Crescent Museum, which is decorated as if a Georgian family still lives there. But honestly, when I go to Bath, I don't want to pack my schedule. I want to amble around, sit in a park, or enjoy a cup of tea with a scone and clotted cream. Barcelona won me over with its tapas and architecture. arcady_31/Getty Images I visited Barcelona during my first trip to Spain . At the time, I knew very little about Spanish history, including architect Antoni Gaudí. However, I felt like he was an invisible host throughout the city, with the buildings he designed peppered all around. One of his greatest works of art, however, is the Sagrada Família — the famous basilica that was recently completed after 144 years of construction. Touring its towers was a highlight of my trip. But what really stuck with me (physically and symbolically) was the cuisine in Barcelona. From the simple pa amb tomàquet (bread with olive oil and tomatoes) to pan-fried Padrón peppers, I found myself constantly on the hunt for my next mini-meal. Digital Finance Analytics defines mortgage stress in cashflow terms — when a household had more outgoings than income — and bases its findings on phone surveys which are then extrapolated using census data. Its analysis for the end of August listed Narre Warren, Cranbourne, Roxburgh Park, Pakenham and Ballarat as the five postcodes with the highest number of affected households in Victoria. Horsham pensioners Annie and Andrew Nikkelson said paying the mortgage was increasingly tough. Peter Norvig, distinguished education fellow at Stanford HAI and former Google research director, used his opening keynote at The AI Conference in San Francisco on Wednesday to speculate on the answer. Almost certainly, it's another AI conference – on Thursday in fact – given the two or three dozen of them that have bubbled up in San Francisco this year or are scheduled in the remaining three months. To get to the present, he took a detour through the past. He acknowledged the milestones of AlexNet and ImageNet in 2012, the Transformer architecture for machine learning in 2017, the debut of ChatGPT in 2022, and the emergence of reasoning and coding agents in 2024. He also touched on the sudden competency of AI models for math, noting that two years ago, GPT-4 couldn't count the number of "r"s in "strawberry." Yet as of August this year, he observed, 25 percent of math preprint papers on arXiv acknowledged AI assistance. Norvig went on to cite Linux kernel creator Linus Torvalds' changing attitude toward AI. "Six months ago he was a skeptic, he became a cautious adopter, and now he's a dogmatic advocate," said Norvig. So what now? Norvig says the process of software engineering needs to change. The tech industry has changed many times before, he said, pointing to transitions from plugging wires into mainframes, to assembly language, to higher level programming languages. "At every step you have to change the way you think about what software engineering is," he said. And now we're going to have to change it all again. How do we do specifications and documentation? How do we capture this theory of the evolving program that we're not capturing well now?" To illustrate that point, Norvig recounted some of his recent work. "I did an embarrassing thing the other day, right? So I'm using Codex, [and I] write some stuff that seems to work," he said. He told Codex to send the pull request for review, and his colleague asked why he was checking in 6,000 temp files. "And I said, 'Well, I didn't notice that,'" Norvig explained. "And sure enough, I had written 6,000 temporary files, and Codex thought that it wanted to check those in. So I told [Codex], 'No, don't check them in, just delete them.' At first I thought, shame on me. I should have looked before I asked for a code review on that. And I just skipped that step of looking. Maybe I should be doing that." Then, said Norvig, he thought that the GPT model should have known that he didn't want to save 6,000 temporary files, so as not to burden the reviewer. And then he mused that if you have enough storage and memory, maybe it would be useful to have those files to have a more thorough history of how the codebase changed. "So the expectations of what's good practice and how that's going to change, that's all going to be different," he said. "We gotta get the security and privacy and data pipelines and supply chains, those are all gonna be different in how they interact with each other," he said. "This idea of continuous integration and recursive self-improvement. How much do we let the systems go off on their own and how are we monitoring them?

( Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon ) Big tech companies wanting to build data centres in Australia would pay a levy to fund the local AI industry under a plan from researchers and unions. The proposal would not seek to build an Australian AI model from scratch but could include a homegrown chatbot like Claude. The Australian AI industry is already struggling to access the level of computing resources needed for frontier development. Tech giants who want to build data centres in Australia would be slugged with a levy to help fund a local artificial intelligence (AI) industry under a plan being pushed by researchers and union figures. In a joint statement, the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) and leading AI academics argue the government must force investment in domestic AI capability and infrastructure, rather than depending on foreign companies to provide access to the technology. The ABC can reveal companies such as US monoliths Anthropic and OpenAI would be required to hand over a portion of their data centre computing capacity in return for developing AI on Australian soil under the proposal. How Australia wants to be more than a data centre host Australia's appeal as a destination for data centres gives it bargaining power in the AI boom. The siphoned "compute", or processing power, would be pooled and distributed by the federal government, while an "AI capability contribution" may also be paid by those same companies to fund the people, software and infrastructure needed to use it. Leading AI researcher Sue Keay from UNSW said Australia did not have a shortage of talent but lacked the "confidence, investment and coordination" to back its own ability. "If AI is going to shape our health care, public services, workplaces and economy, Australians need genuine influence over how those systems are developed, governed and deployed." "Australia has the talent, sector expertise and demand to build substantial AI capability. What it lacks is a funded national ambition and coordinated access to computing resources, skills, research support and patient capital," it reads. Governments in several countries, including the UK, Norway, the US and Korea, have already committed billions to develop publicly owned AI computing resources and infrastructure. Asked on Thursday about the levy proposal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government would "engage constructively with companies, including major ones which are internationally based". "This is a technology that has been driven from US and china, but that's not to say there won't be Australian-based businesses and there are already involved in AI, and there is a real opportunity for Australia," he said. "AI does have risk but it does also have potentially enormous benefits to humankind." Custom AI for the Australian system Under the proposal, framed as the "next logical step", Australia-specific AI would be developed to make work more productive and keep jobs in the country "that would otherwise move overseas". It outlines how investment in a homegrown industry could both safeguard Australian access to the technology and ensure local communities get a return for hosting big tech. "We don't need to build the biggest AI models out there," ACTU assistant secretary Joseph Mitchell said. events.title: OpenAI’s Jev clone could help the frontier lab stop its swarming agents
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. One of the more intriguing announcements at OpenAI’s Dev Day event on Tuesday came in an aside from CEO Sam Altman, who revealed the company’s new “Decisions API.” The API apparently provides similar functionality to Jev , a model released by TypeSafe AI earlier this month that’s explicitly designed for software automation. A kind of super-powered classifier built on an LLM, developers can give Jev a set of choices that it outputs as probabilities cheaply and at high speeds. OpenAI’s Decisions API seems to be the same sort of product. At the event, Altman described the API as a way to give the lab’s Luna model a predefined set of options to choose between, such as categories in which to classify an image or different agent behaviors. “By focusing the model on that choice, we can make it extremely fast while keeping capabilities like image understanding, broad language support, and safety protections,” Altman said. TypeSafe didn’t respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the new product, but CEO Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI engineer who co-invented reinforcement learning, joked on X about the beginning of the clone wars. He added that OpenAI’s interest could be “a sign…that building in a System One compatible way is the future.” (“System One” is TypeSafe’s term of art for fast, intuitive thinking, versus “System 2,” which it applies to deliberate reasoning.) The subtext here is that LLMs as we know them aren’t the right solution for a lot of software because they are comparatively slow and expensive. Developers have been using Jev to augment LLMs and, in doing so, have found that they’re faster and cheaper. It’s not clear how similar Decisions API will be to Jev, since OpenAI released it as a limited preview and, thus far, TechCrunch hasn’t spotted developers running it through its paces. However, there is clearly interest , according to the conversations on X. Decisions API isn’t the only Jev-like API on the internet — other startups are rolling out similar models; OpenAI won’t be the last tech giant to produce one. A key question is how well calibrated each of these decision models’ outputs will be to real life. Almeida says his company’s moat is the synthetic data it creates to generate statistically useful outputs. “Fast and cheap is very easy, you know,” Almeida told TechCrunch last week. “If you want it really fast and cheap, use dice, right? Intelligence is the hard part, and my North Star is always pushing the intelligence-per-dollar Pareto curve.” After just weeks, it seems clear that these models have a future ahead of them, and one likely application is monitoring and securing AI agents. One of OpenAI’s new security measures following a series of incidents where its agents misbehaved on the open internet is using a separate model to watch for bad actions at “significant compute cost.” Shapor Naghibzadeh, a long-time cybersecurity professional who leads the startup QueryStory, thinks that a model like Jev could make that possible far more cheaply. He built a demo for a hackathon held last weekend that uses Jev to check each agentic action against the task it was given, blocking actions it had high confidence were bad, flagging others for review, and permitting the rest. In theory, such monitoring could have stopped the Hugging Face incident — and monitoring of that kind costs $2.94 with Jev, versus $372 with a frontier LLM. A key observation is that Jev is arguably cheap enough to run on every agentic action, which offers a layer of review that could improve the reliability of agents writ large. It’s the kind of thing TypeSafe was hoping to achieve — and now OpenAI has seen the value as well. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Exclusive: HHS launches project to speed up clinical trials
events.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday is launching an effort to reimagine the way clinical trials are designed, with a goal of drastically reducing the time and money it takes to develop new drugs. Why it matters: The program, shared first with Axios, could provide a template for reconfiguring the drug development process and boosting U.S. competitiveness in the global biotech race. Driving the news: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health Director Alicia Jackson are unveiling the new effort in Austin, Texas. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas will also attend the announcement. The effort — dubbed the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program — features teams selected through a bidding process that will bring drug candidates through experimental clinical trial processes. How it works: The initiative under ARPA-H will begin by soliciting ideas from "teams" that include a drug sponsor. Winners will receive funding and support over five years. ARPA-H is looking for proposals that innovate in three technical areas: Phaseless trials that allow faster trials with fewer patients, the ability to analyze data in real time during the trial instead of than only when it ends, and using automation to reduce inefficiencies. Teams will also likely include medical centers or other clinical sites, biostatisticians, and companies that have the ability to predict drug outcomes via a computer. The FDA has been included in the planning of the program, and "there won't be any surprises for regulators in this," said Daria Fedyukina, the program manager. The big picture: One of the reasons China has become such a popular location for drug manufacturers is because it's much cheaper and faster to do early-stage clinical trials there. Experts and the biopharmaceutical community largely agree that in order to compete, the U.S. needs to streamline its trial processes. Today, developing a drug can take longer than a decade and cost around $2 billion. More than 90% of drug candidates fail, according to HHS. What they're saying: "The goal is to develop the tech that is missing and blaze the trail of a new clinical trial paradigm," Fedyukina said. The program will require the development of "blueprints and standards that then can be deployed and used by all other trials in the U.S," she added. While "it's hard to put a number to how much cost savings or time savings we can achieve," Fedyukina said, "there is no reason why we cannot target, let's say, a 10x reduction in the cost of clinical development for a drug." "There's no reason why we cannot cut timeline in half or more," she added. Details: ARPA-H is also announcing three related projects today aimed at improving the infrastructure around clinical trials. One is focused on setting up more clinical trial sites, with the help of AI to speed up site activation and prepare sites that haven't held trials before. This will allow patients who live near hospitals that don't currently participate in clinical trials to gain access to experimental drugs they may benefit from. The other two projects focus on clinical trial data infrastructure and helping patients with complex cancers benefit from their own data and better navigate the care system. The bottom line: This is all an experiment, but if successful it could pay big dividends.

events.title: Doctors condemn big pharma's move to dispense GLP-1s to your door
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Doctors condemn Eli Lilly move to dispense GLP-1 medication Mounjaro direct to door The new Eli Lilly platform negates the need for patients to go into a physical pharmacy. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Eli Lilly's new online platform will dispense certain medicines, starting with Mounjaro, directly to a patient's door. Doctors and pharmacists have criticised the move, arguing it poses a risk to patient safety. Eli Lilly has defended the online platform, saying it does not circumvent pharmacists or GPs, and will improve affordability and convenience for patients. A move by a multi-billion-dollar global pharmaceutical company to bypass bricks-and-mortar pharmacies and deliver its GLP-1 medication directly to consumers' doors has been broadly condemned by doctors and pharmacists, who argue it poses a risk to patient safety. Eli Lilly has announced its new online platform LillyDirect will dispense certain medicines, starting with tirzepatide, an injectable GLP-1 agonist sold as Mounjaro, which is used to treat conditions like type 2 diabetes and obesity. Under the model, patients submit an e-script from their doctor to LillyDirect. The script is then directed to an online third-party pharmacist to dispense, before it is delivered to the patient's home. The pharmaceutical giant said the new platform allowed patients to find competitive pricing without shopping around and it did not replace the need for an independent doctor to prescribe the medication. LillyDirect will dispense certain medicines, starting with tirzepatide, an injectable GLP-1 agonist sold as Mounjaro. ( Reuters: Deena Beasley ) But Royal Australian College of GPs (RACGP) president Michael Wright said GLP-1 agonists were powerful medications with serious side effects, and needed proper oversight and continuity of care. He said using online pharmacists to dispense the medication could remove a layer of protection for patients, noting many might already be using telehealth providers to access the e-script in the first place. "What concerns me about this model is that potentially they can be prescribed in some situations and delivered by someone who doesn't actually have full access to your whole record and I think that really creates risks for patients," Dr Wright said. The Pharmacy Guild of Australia and the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia said the model of care was "clinically inferior" and reduced opportunities for "face-to-face clinical interaction" where problems could be identified and addressed. Trent Twomey (left) is warning against "the Americanisation of Australian health care". ( ABC News: Alice Pavlovic ) "This proposal is a concern to every Australian who values an independent and patient-focused healthcare system," Pharmacy Guild president Trent Twomey said. Eli Lilly advertising online doctors for prescriptions After protracted negotiations with the federal government, Eli Lilly announced in April it would not proceed with the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) listing process, airing a cluster of grievances including that the price Australia was willing to pay for the drug was too low. As a result, Mounjaro can cost patients as much as $700 a month privately. Mounjaro, which is used to treat conditions like type 2 diabetes and obesity, has exploded in popularity. ( ABC News: Evan Young ) Eli Lilly is bound by competition law and is unable to say how much cheaper the medication is when sold through its platform. However, social media users who have already begun using the service, which launched last week, have posted the medication costs as much as $50 less. LillyDirect launched in the US in 2024. There consumers are connected directly with telehealth providers to get their prescription. The Australian Eli Lilly website advertises two major telehealth providers including Juniper, which has previously been criticised by eating disorder experts for aggressive social media marketing of GLP-1 drugs. Michael Wright says GLP-1 agonists are powerful and need proper oversight and continuity of care. ( ABC News ) Dr Wright said GLP-1 drugs were not suitable for everyone, such as those with a history of eating disorders, and came with serious side effects such as the potential risks of suicidal thoughts and behaviours . Telehealth prescribing of weight-loss drugs The ABC has learned of a young woman with anorexia nervosa who was prescribed an GLP-1 drug through a telehealth clinic.

events.title: FTC probes OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR
events.summary: The News The US Federal Trade Commission is investigating top American AI labs — and a prominent safety watchdog — over the potential dangers of their technology. An FTC official confirmed the probe , first reported by the New York Post. The investigation was launched before an unreleased OpenAI model went rogue and hacked open-source AI hub Hugging Face earlier this year, an incident that triggered a fresh wave of concern over the possible harms of uninhibited AI development. In addition to labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, METR, a California-based nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models for risks, is also a target. METR conducted an investigation into the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack and released a report on the incident. The agency is set to send civil investigative demands, which are similar to subpoenas, to the companies in the next few weeks. OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Know More The probe steps up US government scrutiny of top tech companies, even as executives from many of those companies gathered at the White House this week and signed a voluntary pledge to self-police their AI models. US President Donald Trump said the industry was showing “tremendous self-regulation.” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson earlier this month signaled opposition to government regulation driven by AI safety fears, telling Fox News that OpenAI and Anthropic shouldn’t be able to “whip everyone into a panic and then say, ‘We need a whole bunch of regulations that we can comply with.’” He added: “That is how companies build a moat around their businesses to make sure that people can’t compete against them .”

events.title: 3 easy ways to spot a great Indian restaurant, according to a top chef
events.summary: Chef Heena Patel of Besharam in San Francisco shared her tips for finding a great Indian restaurant. Eric Wolfinger Chef Heena Patel of Besharam in San Francisco shared her tips for finding a great Indian restaurant. Patel said you should always try an Indian restaurant that makes its roti and naan in-house. Okra, bitter melon, and opo squash are green flags on any Indian restaurant menu. When Heena Patel first moved to the Bay Area in California , she started selling her homemade Gujarati food at the local farmers market. She'd often come home without making a profit, but she refused to give up on her dream — or her cuisine. Patel is now the James Beard-nominated owner and chef of Besharam , a regional Gujarati restaurant in San Francisco that pays tribute to the dishes of her heritage and childhood. "Just as my guests step outside their comfort zones, I do the same with them, trusting they'll embrace my menu with an open mind," Patel told Business Insider. "That's how I hope to put Gujarati food on the map." Patel also hopes to help diners expand their perception of Indian cuisine. Here are her tips for finding a great Indian restaurant . Okra and bitter melon are green flags Heena Patel is the owner and chef of Besharam in San Francisco. Sarah Felker "Produce like okra, bitter melon, and opo squash are common in Indian cooking," Patel said. "So if you see these ingredients on a menu, you're in for a treat." One of Patel's favorite okra dishes is bhindi masala, which she said "allows okra to shine with its crisp texture." A variety of regional dishes on the menu The malai kofta dish at Besharam. Eric Wolfinger "India has so much to offer, and each dish is rich with history," Patel said. "Growing up, we tried foods from many different regions that have enriched my palate and helped shape me as a chef." "If you see menus that highlight different dishes from various regions in India, it is a good indication that the chef is focused on authentic regional cuisine," she added. When it comes to Gujarati dishes, Patel recommends trying rotla — a traditional flatbread which, unlike naan, is unleavened — and dhokla, a savory sponge cake. For North Indian cuisine, Patel loves sarson ka saag — a Punjabi dish of mustard greens cooked with spices — and the lamb kebabs of Uttar Pradesh. You can't go wrong with vindaloo, a spicy and tangy curry dish from Goa in western India, or sambhar, a lentil-based stew from Tamil Nadu, the southernmost state. Bengal's mishti doi dessert will give you a taste of the east, while chana samosas from Chhattisgarh will take you to India's central region. The bread is key Parathas with raspberry dip at Besharam. Eric Wolfinger "It is definitely worth trying an Indian restaurant that makes rotis and naan in-house," Patel told Business Insider. Indian cuisine also features a variety of flatbreads popular in different regions. Patel recommends trying rotli, paratha, and bhakri. And once you've found a great restaurant, don't play it safe and always stick to the same dishes. "Indian food isn't just about individual dishes; it's about building each bite with different flavors," Patel said. "A curry or a dal on its own is just one part of the experience." "The real magic happens when you layer flavors by adding chutneys, pickles, rotis, and rice," she added. "My advice? Trust your server." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jack Smith faces new lawsuit over congressional phone records
events.summary: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sued former special counsel Jack Smith Wednesday, alleging he unlawfully obtained her cellphone toll records during his investigation of Trump and the 2020 election Why it matters: The lawsuit escalates Republicans' efforts to challenge Smith's investigation more than a year after his probe ended. What they're saying: "Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation's history," Blackburn said. "This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation's justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people. I thank the New Civil Liberties Alliance for their partnership in filing this complaint and for fighting to uphold our cherished constitutional rights." Driving the news: The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee one day after Smith testified at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday. The suit alleges Smith obtained a nondisclosure order without telling the judge that the underlying subpoena sought the records of a sitting senator. Blackburn's cellphone provider was ordered to keep the subpoena secret. Blackburn is asking the court to award her $1 in nominal damages to emphasize that she isn't seeking money but instead wants to hold Smith accountable for his allegedly unlawful actions. Legal counsel for Smith did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Flashback: The lawsuit comes one day after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), a potential running mate for JD Vance in 2028, accused Smith of perjury at Tuesday's hearing but got his facts wrong and was later corrected by Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). The mistake went viral and drew extensive criticism on social media. Catch up quick: In October 2025, the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee released highly redacted documents showing that the FBI had investigated approximately 160 Republican figures as part of its probe into Trump's false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. The probe, known as Arctic Frost, sought to identify those who "conspired to corruptly obstruct the United States Congress' certification of the 2020 Presidential election results by submitting allegedly fraudulent elector certificates." By the numbers: The lawsuit claims the Arctic Frost probe subpoenaed records associated with at least 20 Republican members of Congress. The lawsuit claims about 400 Republican individuals and organizations were targeted. The lawsuit says records involving roughly 4,782 Trump donors, including 102 Tennesseans, contained home addresses, bank account numbers and signatures. The bottom line: Blackburn's lawsuit extends the legal and political fight over the Justice Department's investigations into Trump after he left office. Trump and his allies have vowed to continue probing those who investigated or crossed the president, including New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), former FBI chief James Comey and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). Go deeper: Jan. 6 probe potentially investigated over 150 Republicans, documents show

events.title: Everything we know about 'Fourth Wing' book 4, from Rebecca Yarros' hints to new clues in 'Threshing Day'
events.summary: Rebecca Yarros is working on the fourth "Empyrean" novel. Casey Paul/MLB Photos via Getty Images Rebecca Yarros brought readers back into her "Empyrean" universe with "Threshing Day." The collection of stories offers clues about the series' future, which ended on a cliffhanger. The author has also shared hints about how Violet Sorrengail's story will continue in interviews. Rebecca Yarros' next "Fourth Wing" book is out, but it's not the fourth novel in the "Empyrean" series. It's been over a year since Yarros released "Onyx Storm," which continues the story of Violet Sorrengail's journey to become a dragon rider and fight forces of dark magic at Basgiath War College after books one and two in the series, " Fourth Wing " and " Iron Flame." The series is set to comprise five novels, all published by Entangled's fantasy imprint, Red Tower. "Onyx Storm" — the fastest-selling adult novel released in 20 years — ended on a cliffhanger, so Yarros' readers have been clamoring to get their hands on the next romantasy novel in the series since the moment they finished book three. Yarros has confirmed on Instagram that she is writing book four, but it will still be a while before it's published. However, on Tuesday, Yarros released a collection of short stories set in the "Empyrean" universe, "Threshing Day," giving readers a taste of what the future of her series may hold. Keep reading for a rundown of everything we know about "Empyrean" book four and how "Threshing Day" fits into the series. Warning: The rest of this article has spoilers for the "Empyrean" series, including "Threshing Day." Yarros started writing the fourth 'Empyrean' novel in March 2026 Yarros released the first three books in the "Empyrean" series in under two years. "Fourth Wing" came out in April 2023, "Iron Flame" was released in October 2023, and "Onyx Storm" hit shelves in January 2025. Yarros made clear she wouldn't be writing book four at the same pace. Speaking at an engagement in Philadelphia on January 25, 2025, Yarros said she wouldn't commit to a release date, as she was planning to write a contemporary novel first. Yarros later  told Elle  that she intended to rest before returning to writing in part because the amount of work she did in recent years wasn't good for her mentally or physically, as she has chronic medical conditions, including Ehlers-Danlos  syndrome, a connective tissue disorder, and  POTS, an autonomic nervous system disorder . She kept her word, keeping largely quiet about book four for the rest of 2025. Then, on February 8, 2026, she shared on Instagram that she had begun plotting, and on March 19, 2026, she posted a Reel announcing she had begun writing the next "Empyrean" novel. Rebecca Yarros. Rebecca Yarros/Red Tower Books In the Reel , Yarros walks up to a board and writes "#4" at the top. "And now that my latest contemporary novel is off to my editor, I'm back writing in the Empyrean world for the foreseeable future," Yarros captioned the post. "Let's ride." The author has posted a few updates about her progress since then, most notably on June 13. She shared a short video clip on Instagram of an ocean view and said in her caption that she would be spending the summer writing at the beach. "Our home is undergoing distractingly noisy work, which gives us the perfect excuse to pack up our kids and spend the summer on Deverelli time while I'm writing book 4," she said. Deverelli is an isle that Violet visits in "Onyx Storm," and it plays a key role in the book's plot. It will still be a while before the fourth "Empyrean" book hits bookshelves, but fans can rest assured that Yarros will be focused on the novel in the coming months. The fourth book will hopefully address unanswered questions from 'Onyx Storm' There was no shortage of drama at the end of "Onyx Storm." First, Xaden took more power from the earth, speeding up his transition into a dark magic-wielding venin, one of the main antagonists in the series, and sending him down a path toward evil. Another unnamed dragon rider turned venin as well. One of Violet's dragons, Andarna, returned to her after her time away with the irid dragons, and Violet woke up with a wedding ring and blessing of her marriage to Xaden from the goddess Dunne, with no memory of the last 12 hours of her life. In the book's final line, her fellow rider Imogen Cardulo reveals she used her signet power to wipe Violet's memory of the night — at her request. Violet's brother, Brennan, also revealed that six dragon eggs and four riders, including Xaden and his best friend, Garrick Tavis, are missing. "Onyx Storm" by Rebecca Yarros. Red Tower Hopefully, the fourth book in the "Empyrean" series will reveal what happened between Violet and Xaden, where Xaden and the other missing riders are, the location of the missing eggs, what Andarna learned from her time with the irids, and how Xaden's additional use of his venin powers harmed his soul. Likewise, Violet will likely still be searching for a cure to save Xaden from being venin, but as his wife, she also becomes the Duchess of Tyrrendor. She will have new power and responsibility in his absence, and readers will have to wait to see how she balances her new role as she develops her signets . Hints from 'Threshing Day' On September 29, 2026, Yarros released a new "Empyrean" collection called "Threshing Day." It tells the stories of 13 cadets at Basgiath as they bond with their dragons in the high-stakes, often life-threatening experience known as Threshing. Violet made history as the first rider to bond two dragons on her Threshing Day in "Fourth Wing." Most of the "Empyrean" series is told from Violet's point of view, but Yarros said during an appearance on the "Fantasy Fangirls" podcast in October 2025 that she plans for the fourth installment to be told from multiple perspectives, including the character Sloane Mairi specifically. "Threshing Day" offers a bridge to those new perspectives, as all the featured riders are characters who could tell future "Fourth Wing" stories, like Sloane, Xaden, and Imogen. The collection also addressed a plot device Yarros has used in the novels. After riders bond a dragon, the rider announces the dragon's name to the Scribes so it can be recorded, rather than the dragons communicating directly with the Scribes. Yarros previously said that creates the possibility that the dragons or riders are lying about their identities. It is forbidden for riders to bond with their direct ancestors' dragons, as it allows riders to develop second signets. In the text, it appeared like some dragons wanted to bond with the children or grandchildren of rebels they had worked with in the past, skirting the rules. However, it wasn't clear how that worked until "Threshing Day." "Threshing Day" by Rebecca Yarros. The investigation by the Federal Trade Commission is the first official US enforcement ⁠action that delves into rogue AI agents, following a surge in incidents first reported in July that have stoked fears among the public that uncontrolled AI could one day ⁠harm humans. The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top ​AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research ‌group Metr, according to multiple reports . Anthropic and ‌OpenAI have used Metr to conduct independent investigations into security incidents involving their agentic AI technology. Anthropic, OpenAI and ‌Metr did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The New York Post first reported the news. Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, had concerns about the companies before AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. The incident, in which OpenAI agents probed the AI coding hub for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack, sparked global discussion of the issue. Ferguson suggested last week in an interview that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any ​harm they cause. The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI, Ferguson said at an event in Austin. The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to ⁠take reasonable measures to secure consumers’ data. Donald Trump met with top ​AI executives on Tuesday, where the ​companies agreed to establish voluntary standards. events.title: No 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EU
events.summary: Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU. Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto. Some in No 10 are keen to promise that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has previously said he wants to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader. Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader to announce a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely. The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.” On Wednesday he clarified that this would include an option to rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer. Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union , we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way .” Burnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents. Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.” The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto. Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion. Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology. On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin. Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so. Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe. The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party. No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it. Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession. But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday welcomed Burnham’s comments . “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday. He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.” An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union . It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.

Meyer, with defrauding investors and MGM-managed funds in connection with investments in SpaceX and other pre-IPO securities. According to the SEC’s complaint, in a series of schemes from at least December 2021 to the present, the defendants violated their fiduciary duties by misusing client fund assets, and lied to the underlying investors in the funds. In at least three of those schemes, the defendants allegedly misappropriated client assets from certain MGM-managed funds to pay for Meyer’s personal expenses. As outlined in the complaint, the defendants concealed their actions in one scheme by sending statements to investors that inflated their account values. The complaint also alleges that, in one of the misappropriation schemes involving three MGM-managed funds, defendants misappropriated portions of investor proceeds and required investors to sign releases accepting distributions of amounts that were less than they were owed in order to get any money at all. Finally, the complaint alleges that defendants repeatedly failed to address a capital call deficiency owed by an MGM-managed fund in connection with its investment in SpaceX, resulting in the fund forfeiting its nearly $3,000,000 investment. “This case is a reminder that fraudsters can exploit the allure of exclusive, high-return pre-IPO access to take advantage of retail investors,” said Corey A. Schuster, Chief of the Enforcement Division’s Asset Management Unit. “The defendants in this matter were investment advisers entrusted with acting as fiduciaries to their clients. Nevertheless, they allegedly engaged in multiple fraudulent acts to enrich themselves.” The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, charges the defendants with violating antifraud provisions of the Advisers Act of 1940. The SEC seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against both defendants, as well as a conduct-based injunction against Meyer. events.title: 16-year-old researcher found a Microsoft bug, got admin access to databases with 17.3 trillion rows
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters It's 2 am. Do you know what your teen is doing? Azure maintenance mess disrupted hybrid clouds, VPNs, cloudy VMware services 8 hours ago Drunk Van Halen fan called Microsoft support and demanded to speak to Gates 20 hours ago Microsoft sends PDFs to strange new worlds instead of SharePoint 1 day ago Redmond to millions of Power BI users: You’re Fabric app devs now 1 day ago What eldritch horror lurks behind Heathrow's information screens? 1 day ago A 16-year-old security researcher named Faav found an authentication flaw in Microsoft’s Titan analytics service that allowed him to gain administrator access, submit unauthorized SQL queries with no valid credentials, and potentially reach analytics databases containing an estimated 17.3 trillion stored rows. Titan is an internal analytics platform, and Redmond restricts access via its web interface to Microsoft employees. Faav, with an assist from an AI hackbot he built called Antares, found that he could access Titan’s API through an Azure Cloud Services host because Titan didn’t check the signature on a login token. Microsoft has since locked down the API and paid Faav a $5,000 bug bounty for his research. He says the breakthrough came after 10 days of authentication errors, when he returned to the problem after finishing Friday’s schoolwork and finally managed to execute SQL as a Titan admin after 1 AM Saturday. “It was 2 AM,” Faav said in a blog about his findings. “I wanted to yell, or at least say something out loud, but my parents were asleep. So I just sat there staring at 17,333,335,124,315 and checked the math again.” He also notes that he rewrote his blog post at Microsoft’s request, cut sections and numbers, and reworded the impact prior to publication. “We appreciate the opportunity to investigate the findings reported by Faav,” Microsoft said in a statement provided to Faav for his blog. “Their submission and coordinated vulnerability disclosure helped us to better protect our customers by hardening our services. We value and appreciate safe security research under the terms of the Microsoft Bug Bounty Program and look forward to continuing to work with Faav in the future.” The research began on August 25 when Antares found Titan’s public API. For the next 10 days, the human and bot tested the service’s JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication checks and email-formatted user principal names (UPNs), eventually finding an unsigned token that could reach Titan’s local user lookup - but not a UPN that Titan recognized. Early on September 5, Faav changed the unsigned token’s UPN from an email-formatted identity to admin. Titan recognized it as a local username, resolved it to local user ID 1, which held an admin role, and allowed him to run SQL. The takeaway, according to Faav: Titan validated the contents of the JWT (tenant, audience, app ID, user) but never verified the signature, the most important part of any authentication check. The authentication checks felt like a hotel where every door had a working keycard reader, but any keycard unlocked any room. Despite all the access-control logic existing in the app, the one missing piece made it all pointless. If you’re a developer (or coding agent) reading this, the most important takeaway from this post is to make sure you verify signatures above all else when building auth. This gave Faav access to Titan’s platform metadata database, and from there he could query application tables directly. The metadata contained: About 25,000 account and email records. 15,001 employee organization records. 20,979 virtual-dataset SQL definitions. 24,569 dashboards, 425,891 charts, and 27,347 dataset definitions. Titan’s user and usage directory exposed employee job titles, departments, and management hierarchy, which the researcher notes could be useful for social-engineering attacks - “though I never tested or demonstrated that,” he added.

events.title: The most iconic burger joint in every state
events.summary: From classic diners to drive-thrus, here are the most iconic burger restaurants across the country. bhofack2/Getty Images/iStockphoto Great burger joints can be found in every corner of the country. We found the most famous burger restaurants nationwide based on local lore and reviews. From nostalgic drive-ins to local institutions, here's the most iconic burger joint in every state. Fire up the grill or hit the road — few foods are more quintessentially American than a great burger. We found the most iconic or best-known burger joints in every state, from nationally known institutions like In-N-Out Burger in California to tiny roadside stands that have become local legends. Our list includes burger destinations with historical or regional significance and devoted local or national followings. Many have been serving their signature patties for decades, earned major accolades, or been featured on TV — proof that an unforgettable burger can be found in every corner of the country. Here's the most iconic burger joint in every state. ALABAMA: Vicki's Lunch Van in Montgomery Vicki's Lunch Van. Jamie V./Yelp Vicki's Lunch Van isn't much to look at from the outside, but that's part of the charm of this no-frills Montgomery institution. Open since 2003, it's best known for thick, hand-patted burgers that are much bigger than you'd expect from a place called a lunch van, served simply with classic toppings and golden fries. ALASKA: Arctic Roadrunner in Anchorage Arctic Roadrunner. Andrew H./Yelp Arctic Roadrunner has been feeding Anchorage since 1964, when Richard Sanchis started selling cheeseburgers from a trailer before opening a permanent restaurant. Its burgers feature names inspired by the state, such as the Kenai Whopper and Kodiak Islander, while longtime customers can even earn a spot in the restaurant's photo gallery, which spans over 20 years of visits. ARIZONA: The Chuckbox in Tempe The Chuck Box. Travis T./Yelp The Chuckbox has been grilling burgers in Tempe since 1972, and thankfully, not much has changed. Burgers are still cooked over an open mesquite fire, giving them their signature smoky char, and the restaurant remains cash-only. Locals recommend the Tijuana Torpedo, topped with jalapeño jack cheese and green chile, for a burger with distinctly Southwestern heat. ARKANSAS: Hugo's in Fayetteville Hugo's. Paige C./Yelp You have to head underground to find one of Arkansas' most beloved burgers. Located in a basement just off Fayetteville's historic square since 1977, Hugo's has become a longtime hangout for generations of University of Arkansas students. Its burgers, homemade fries, beer-cheese soup, and famously retro atmosphere have helped make the restaurant a Fayetteville institution. CALIFORNIA: In-N-Out Burger in Baldwin Park In-N-Out Burger. Erin McDowell/Business Insider California's most iconic burger is also one of its most widely available — at least in the state; not so much elsewhere in the country. Harry and Esther Snyder opened the first location in Baldwin Park in 1948, where the restaurant's two-way speaker system helped pioneer the drive-thru ordering experience. More than 75 years later, the tiny menu, Double-Double, Animal Style fries, and red-and-yellow branding are practically synonymous with Southern California. COLORADO: My Brother's Bar in Denver My Brother's Bar. John C./Yelp My Brother's Bar has only had its current name since 1970, but people have been drinking at its Denver address since 1873, making it one of the city's oldest continuously operating bars. Today, it's nearly as famous for burgers like the three-cheese Johnny Burger and buffalo-bison Ralphie burger as it is for its lengthy history. CONNECTICUT: Louis' Lunch in New Haven Louis' Lunch. Nolan F./Yelp Louis' Lunch has one of the strongest claims to inventing the hamburger, so naming it Connecticut's most iconic burger joint was a no-brainer. The Lassen family says Louis Lassen first put ground steak between slices of toast for a customer in a rush way back in 1900. The restaurant still cooks its burgers in antique vertical broilers and serves them on toast with only cheese, tomato, or onion available as toppings. DELAWARE: The Charcoal Pit in Wilmington Charcoal Pit. Wilton P./Yelp The Charcoal Pit looks like the kind of burger joint you'd see in a 1950s movie … except it really has been around since 1956. Flame-broiled burgers, triple-spun milkshakes, red booths, and a giant neon sign have made the local restaurant a nostalgic favorite for generations of Delaware diners. The restaurant's customers over the years have included US presidents, including Barack Obama and Delaware native Joe Biden, who has been going for years. FLORIDA: El Cap in St. Petersburg El Cap Restaurant. Michelle T./Yelp There are plenty of flashy places to grab a burger in Florida, but El Cap has become a St. Petersburg favorite by being pretty much the opposite. The old-school neighborhood joint keeps its burgers straightforward, serving thin patties with classic toppings like lettuce and tomato alongside pints of ice-cold beer. GEORGIA: Holeman and Finch in Atlanta Holeman and Finch Public House. King R./Yelp Holeman and Finch turned its burger into an Atlanta legend by making it almost impossible to get at first. After opening in 2008, the restaurant famously served just 24 burgers at 10 p.m. each night, prompting crowds to gather for a chance to try it. The double cheeseburger became so popular that it eventually made its way onto the regular menu. HAWAII: Teddy's Bigger Burgers in Honolulu Teddy's Bigger Burgers. Jen K./Yelp Teddy's Bigger Burgers grew out of backyard cookouts before founders Ted Tsakiris and Rich Stula opened their first restaurant near Diamond Head in 1998. The homegrown chain became known for big, charbroiled burgers topped with everything from avocado to grilled pineapple. After decades of local "best burger" recognition and expansion beyond Hawaii, Teddy's remains one of the islands' biggest burger success stories. IDAHO: Hudson's Hamburgers in Coeur d'Alene Hudson's Hamburgers. Jennifer T./Yelp Hudson's Hamburgers has been keeping things simple since Harley Hudson opened his first burger stand in Coeur d'Alene in 1907. The menu has barely changed in more than a century: Burgers come with pickles and onions, and you still won't find fries or milkshakes. Five generations of the Hudson family have worked the grill, making this tiny counter spot a piece of Idaho history. ILLINOIS: Au Cheval in Chicago Au Cheval. Jenni W./Yelp Au Cheval has only been around since 2012, but its burger didn't need long to become a Chicago icon. Bon Appétit raved about it almost immediately, calling the griddled burger — stacked with American cheese, Dijonnaise, and pickles — potentially its favorite in the country and "just about perfect." The resulting hype helped turn long waits into part of the Au Cheval experience. INDIANA: Powers Hamburge

events.title: How Ben Shelton uses creatine, protein, and one brutal deep core exercise to build power
events.summary: Tennis phenom Ben Shelton claimed victory after a four-hour marathon match at the 2026 US Open. He said his training for stamina and explosive power paid off. Photo by Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP via Getty Images Tennis phenom Ben Shelton said his training focuses on exercises for stability and explosive power. He said suffering through split squats and Copenhagen planks makes it easy to keep up on the court. His supplement stack has some gym bro favorites like creatine. For nearly four and a half hours, Ben Shelton battled Spain's Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinals marathon. More than a million viewers tuned in to the late-night match, one of the most-watched at the 2026 US Open . Fans were on the edge of their seats until around 3:30 a.m. on September 9, when the American finally claimed victory. Some joked about calling in sick to work after. For Shelton, it was "another day at the office." "The more you build up your match count, you build up your tolerance to playing that long; it starts to feel normal," he told Business Insider. The 23-year-old, coached by his dad, former ATP champ Bryan Shelton, went pro in 2022 and now ranks fourth in the world. Shelton has no plans to slow down, he said in our interview about his partnership with Thorne supplements . For the rising star, career longevity is as much a priority as winning matches now. He shared details of his intense training regimen and how every set, rep, and drill is an investment in the long game. "Many of the decisions that we make are choices not just for today, but for a long-term goal," Shelton said. "I know I'm not in my prime yet. I know I'm building toward something." Exercises for explosive power For a pro tennis player, Shelton was late to the sport. He grew up trying a little of everything — football, baseball, basketball, and swimming. It turns out to be an advantage, helping him build a versatile skillset before specializing in tennis. His current training builds on his well-rounded athletic foundation by focusing on specific movement patterns for his tennis game. That means a lot of single-sided exercises, like Bulgarian split squats, to hone balance and power on one leg at a time, ideal for agility. "Bulgarians," as Shelton calls them, are perfect if you like feeling the burn. To do them, elevate one foot behind you onto a bench or box, bend the standing leg to 90 degrees, then straighten it, keeping your torso upright and engaging the glutes and quads. For more of a challenge, hold a weight, such as a dumbbell or kettlebell, in one or both hands. To cultivate explosive power, Shelton uses plyometric moves like mini-hurdle hops and box jumps. Both types of exercise help ensure he has the engine to power through long, grueling sessions on the court. He also takes his core training and stability seriously, repping out his "least favorite exercise in the world," the Copenhagen plank, to work the hip adductors, obliques, and deep abs. It's a brutal variation on a side plank that involves balancing your top leg on a bench and lifting your hips to create a straight line from your foot to your shoulder. The bottom leg hovers under the bench — you need to use your inner thigh muscles to keep it off the ground. "No matter how many times you do them, they still suck," Shelton said. "If you're going to be a pro athlete, you've got to be used to doing things that you don't enjoy." The isometric hold in the plank — creating muscle tension from a static position — helps to strengthen small stabilizer muscles, joints, and tendons to prevent injury. "A lot of serious injuries start with small ones or start with a different part of the body that makes you compensate," Shelton said. "Staying on top of the little things is really important." Shelton's muscle-building supplement stack Off the court and outside the gym, Shelton said he focuses on the basics like good sleep and good nutrition. From there, he said, adding supplements gives him an extra edge that adds up to better performance over time. "When you are consistent and build up over months or years, it really does start making a huge difference," he said. Shelton's supplement stack includes: Whey protein: a convenient, easily-digestible strategy to get enough protein for muscle growth and recovery. Creatine powder : an affordable, multi-purpose boost to the body's energy stores to support muscle-building and brain health. Magnesium: a mineral that helps regulate the nervous system, supporting healthy sleep. Electrolytes: to replenish the nutrients lost through sweating to prevent dehydration and muscle cramps. Daily multivitamin: as insurance against nutritional deficiencies and to shore up the immune system. Down time: watching movies and workout dates Shelton's schedule isn't all business. In his free time, he indulges in being a bit of a couch potato. "I'm a homebody," he said. "I've watched more movies this year than probably anybody. I'm a pretty simple person." He also unwinds by spending quality time with his girlfriend, Trinity Rodman, of the US Women's National Team. Tennis and soccer have similar off-seasons, so the pair use that time to work out together, in addition to supporting each other at competitions. "I'll come out to her practice and play soccer with her, and she'll come out to mine and play tennis, and it's really enjoyable to be able to experience those things together," Shelton said. "I've learned from her how to enjoy myself more and take myself less seriously at times." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: What's inside the Trump administration's $27bn portfolio?
events.summary: The US is building a growing portfolio of investments in private companies, with President Donald Trump 's administration signing 39 deals valued at $27.7 billion since January 2025. These deals, according to analysis from the Council on Foreign Relations, have been shaped across several agencies in Washington, including the Commerce Department, the Pentagon and the Development Finance Corporation. A separate report by the Cato Institute recorded 30 deals, but the conservative think tank did not include deals struck by the DFC in its own calculations, citing a 2018 law that authorised the DFC to make equity investments years before the second Trump administration. Mr Trump has framed these agreements as being of vital importance to US national security. The administration's most prominent investment has been Intel , and the US government announced in August 2025 that it had taken a roughly 10 per cent stake for $8.9 billion in the computer chip designer and fabricator. The purchase was made with funding from $5.7 billion in previously unused grants from the Biden-era Chips Act . Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan at the time said Mr Trump's focus on chip manufacturing was bringing significant investment to a sector that is vital to US “economic and national security”. The deal was struck weeks after the President called for the Intel boss's resignation on accusations of alleged ties to China. While historic, the announcement also showed how the US government has been integrating equity deals into its investment arsenal that also includes loans and grants. Minerals and metals The administration has aggressively pursued ownership in minerals and metals companies as part of a broader push to shore up domestic supply chains to loosen China's grip on materials necessary to build out defence munitions and advanced technologies. In July 2025, the Defence Department announced it was taking a $400 million equity stake in MP Materials as part of a public-private partnership. The department, through its partnership with MP, later that year established a joint venture with Saudi mining company Maaden that would build a rare earth refinery in the kingdom. The Commerce and Energy Departments in January this year announced a $280 million deal with MP rival USA Rare Earth for up to $1.6 billion under the Chips programme. Over the last year, the US government has also taken up stakes in the magnet maker Vulcan Elements, minerals exploration company Trilogy Metals and Lithium Americas, which is developing a massive lithium mine in Nevada. Meanwhile, the DFC signed a $565 million loan agreement with Brazilian rare earths miner Serra Verde, which included the option to take a minority equity stake. The DFC this year also closed on its $600 million investment in the Orion Critical Mineral Consortium , a public-private partnership that aims to invest in critical minerals projects. The initiative is a joint effort with Orion Resources and Abu Dhabi's ADQ. The Trump administration also announced a so-called golden share in its acquisition of US Steel/Nippon Steel under the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS). Semiconductors In addition to its $8.9 billion stake in Intel, the US holds investments in 10 other semiconductor companies which it used under the authority of the Chips Act, according to CFR's analysis. Among them is GlobalFoundries . The New York-headquartered company signed a letter of intent with the Commerce Department in January for a $300 million award to accelerate the development of next-generation silicon photonics. Abu Dhabi's Mubadala owns roughly 73 per cent of the semiconductor manufacturer. The Commerce Department also used its Chips authority on investments in companies to hold non-controlling stakes in Aeluma, Extropic, I-Pulse and others. Aeluma, Extropic and GlobalFoundries were among the six chipmakers the US government added to its portfolio in July. Other investments In April, L3Harris announced its missile-making unit had closed a $1 billion strategic investment deal with the Defence Department. L3Harris said it will continue to hold a more than 80 per cent stake in the new missile solutions business. And in August, the White House announced a deal with the US-backed North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second-largest private oil producer in Venezuela, and the interim government in Caracas. Under the agreement, Venezuela's interim authorities authorised Nabep 100-year concessions for 17 oilfields in the country. The company has granted the Defence Department's Office of Strategic Control a 35 per cent equity stake in its corporate parent, according to the White House.

events.title: Russia launches major attack on Ukraine's energy grid as winter looms
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Russia launches major attack on Ukraine's energy grid as winter looms, seven killed Russia carried out strikes across Kyiv and many other cities across Ukraine. ( Reuters: Gleb Garanich ) Russia has carried out its heaviest wave of attacks on Ukraine's energy grid in months, ahead of what is expected to be a bitterly cold winter for many in the war-torn country. At least seven people were killed in the strikes, which followed days of drone attacks on Kyiv. Emergency power cuts were in operation, causing some tram services in Kyiv to be suspended. Russia has unleashed a widely anticipated air campaign against Ukraine's energy grid, hitting power facilities and infrastructure around Kyiv and other regions in the heaviest combined attack on energy sites in months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, while visiting the eastern front on Wednesday, said seven people, including a child, were killed in the attacks. It followed days of intensifying drone barrages primarily on the capital, a prelude to what many Ukrainians expect to be a winter of attacks intended to plunge cities into cold and darkness. Ukraine's state power grid operator Ukrenergo said it had imposed its first emergency power cuts since spring as a result of the attack in Kyiv and three surrounding regions. Kyiv authorities said the strikes damaged a key power plant and other energy facilities around the capital. The attacks on a Kyiv power plant threw smoke across the Ukrainian capital's skyline. ( Reuters: Gleb Garanich ) Russian attacks last winter, which brought record-low temperatures, ravaged power and heating systems, forcing Ukrainians to adapt to dire circumstances. Some of the capital's tram and trolleybus services ground to a halt due to the outages on Wednesday, local time, as people headed home from work. "Russia has escalated to massive strikes on energy infrastructure," Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said on X after the attacks overnight. "Since summer, there's barely been a day without an attack on our energy infrastructure. But a combined strike of this scale hasn't happened since the end of last heating season." President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said energy infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding area was the main target of an onslaught that included nearly 190 drones and ballistic missiles. The air force said it had downed 5 missiles and 155 drones. A child was among the seven dead across Ukraine, Mr Zelenskyy said, with critical infrastructure coming under attack in five regions. Other damage was reported in another five regions, he added. Russia has been exploiting a shortage of Ukrainian interceptors by launching nightly missile salvos. ( Reuters: Valentyn Ogirenko ) Russia said its forces had struck power plants in the Kyiv region, an industrial complex in Odesa region, and port infrastructure in Ismail in the southwest. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said debris had been found at a Western embassy, but offered no further details. The overnight attack triggered a more than 12-hour air-raid alert. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described Wednesday's attack by Russia as a "deliberate" distraction from its grinding battlefield offensive in eastern Ukraine, which has slowed since last year. Ukrainian state weather forecasters say they expect freezing temperatures at night in Kyiv in the coming days.

events.title: Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns
events.summary: Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday. For over a year, Donald Trump has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair Jerome Powell around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that was dropped in April. The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation. “At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said. Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018bn by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027. The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be non-partisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail. Trump latched on to the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features including a VIP dining room and a garden terrace. In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s. Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures. “It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.” The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said. Get the most important news as it breaks Soon after, Trump turned his Fed fight toward Fed governor Lisa Cook, whom he tried to fire over mortgage fraud. The supreme court ruled earlier this summer that the firing was unconstitutional because the White House did not follow proper procedure. In January, Powell released a stunning video statement announcing that the Department of Justice was investigating the renovations as part of a criminal investigation, noting that the investigation was “pretext” for the Fed not lowering interest rates. “This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions – or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation,” Powell said at the time. The justice department investigation would end up stalling the confirmation of current Fed chair Kevin Warsh , after a key Republican senator said he would be a holdout until the department ended its investigation. In April, the justice department closed the investigation. Trump and his economic advisers have continued to call for the Fed to lower interest rates, though the Fed most recently hiked rates , citing high inflation.
